core.summary:
Achilles Tatius (Ἀχιλλεὺς Τάτιος, Achilleus Tatios, 2nd century CE) was, according to the Byzantine Suda, from Alexandria. The Suda's further claims, that he became a Christian and a bishop and wrote on astronomy, are probably later confusions. Papyri show that his novel was being read in Egypt by the late second century CE.

Leucippe and Clitophon (Τὰ κατὰ Λευκίππην καὶ Κλειτοφῶντα, Ta kata Leukippēn kai Kleitophōnta), in eight books, is told in the first person by Clitophon, whom the author meets at Sidon in front of a painting of Europa and the bull. Clitophon falls in love with his cousin Leucippe, elopes with her, and suffers shipwreck, bandits, apparent deaths (Leucippe 'dies' three times), a rival marriage and a trial before the lovers are reunited at Ephesus. The tone is often knowing and comic. The narrator is no model of fidelity, and the novel plays with the conventions that Chariton and Xenophon took seriously.

Achilles Tatius is a writer of the Second Sophistic, and his Greek is polished Attic. He fills the story with learned digressions on love, animals, painting and natural wonders, and with ecphrases (ἔκφρασις, ekphrasis, "description") of works of art. His prose, full of balanced antitheses and short rhythmic clauses, was much admired in Byzantium, although Photius disapproved of its indecency.
timeline: Leucippe and Clitophon written (2nd century CE)
Papyri show the novel circulating in Egypt (late 2nd century)
Photius praises the style but condemns the morals of the novel (9th century)
The Suda makes him a Christian and a bishop, probably a later confusion (10th century)
Annibale della Croce's Latin translation of the whole novel
Editio princeps of the Greek text (Heidelberg, Commelinus)
core.manuscripts: Leucippe and Clitophon survives in some twenty manuscripts, far more than Chariton or Xenophon, a sign of its popularity in Byzantium. They fall into two main families. Several papyri of the second to fourth centuries, including one that arranges the text in a different order, show that the ancient text was already somewhat fluid.
core.variants: Editors must choose between the two manuscript families, which differ in many small details. One papyrus places a passage from Book 2 earlier in the story, and scholars debate whether this reflects an earlier version or an error. The date of the novel was once put much later, until the papyri fixed it in the second century.

core.summary:
Aeschines (Αἰσχίνης, Aischinēs, c. 390–c. 314 BCE) rose from modest beginnings to become one of the leading politicians of Athens. According to Demosthenes' hostile portrait, his father kept a school and he himself worked as a clerk and as a minor tragic actor before entering politics; he also served as a soldier. In 346 he went with Demosthenes on the embassies that negotiated the Peace of Philocrates with Philip II of Macedon, and he became the chief spokesman for accommodation with Macedon, and Demosthenes' bitterest rival.

Only three of his speeches survive, which ancient critics called 'the Graces'. Each belongs to his long duel with Demosthenes. Against Timarchus (346/5) destroyed one of Demosthenes' allies by accusing him of prostitution in his youth. On the Embassy (343) was his successful defence against Demosthenes' charge that he had betrayed Athens on the embassy to Philip; he was acquitted by a narrow margin. Against Ctesiphon (330) attacked the proposal to crown Demosthenes. Demosthenes answered with On the Crown, and Aeschines won less than a fifth of the votes, left Athens, and taught rhetoric on Rhodes. He is said to have died on Samos. The twelve letters under his name are later forgeries.

Ancient critics admired his natural fluency, clarity and vivid narrative. His Greek is clear, lively Attic, with long quotations of laws, decrees and poetry and a showman's ear for effect. Read alongside Demosthenes, the speeches give both sides of the great political argument of fourth-century Athens.
timeline: Born in Athens (c. 390)
Serves as a soldier and begins his political career
Serves with Demosthenes on the embassies to Philip; the Peace of Philocrates
Against Timarchus (346/5)

First printed in the Aldine Orators (Venice)
core.manuscripts: The three speeches survive in a good number of medieval manuscripts, which editors divide into several families, with ancient commentaries (scholia) in the margins. Papyri from Egypt add early evidence. The letters survive in a separate tradition.
core.variants: As with Demosthenes, the documents quoted in the speeches (laws and decrees) are often later insertions rather than the texts Aeschines had read out. The manuscript families differ in many small readings, and some passages have been expanded by later hands. The twelve letters are not authentic.

core.summary:
Aeschylus (Αἰσχύλος, Aischylos, c. 525–456 BCE) is the earliest of the three great Athenian tragedians and the first whose plays survive. He fought against the Persians at Marathon, and by some ancient accounts at Salamis too. The epitaph that tradition attributes to him remembers Marathon, not his plays. He wrote between seventy and ninety plays (the ancient sources differ) and, according to the ancient Life, won thirteen victories in his lifetime. Seven tragedies survive under his name, one of them, Prometheus Bound, of disputed authorship.

Aristotle (Poetics 1449a) credits him with adding a second actor, which made real dialogue and conflict possible on stage; by the Oresteia he was also using the third actor introduced by Sophocles. His Persians (472 BCE) is the earliest surviving tragedy that can be dated securely, and the only surviving one about a recent historical event. The Suppliants was long thought older still, until a papyrus published in 1952 showed that it was probably produced in the 460s. The Oresteia (458 BCE), made up of Agamemnon, Libation Bearers and Eumenides, is the only complete trilogy to survive (its satyr play, Proteus, is lost). It follows a cycle of murder and revenge in the house of Atreus to its end in a court of law at Athens.

His language is dense, bold and full of striking images and coinages. In Aristophanes' Frogs (405 BCE) Euripides mocks his "ox-sized words" (ῥήματα βόεια, rhēmata boeia), and a single sentence of the Agamemnon can call Helen "ship-destroying, man-destroying, city-destroying" (ἑλέναυς, ἕλανδρος, ἑλέπτολις, helenaus, helandros, heleptolis, 689–90), a pun on her name. Like all tragedians he gives his choral songs a Doric colouring, with ᾱ where Attic has η (μάτηρ, matēr, for μήτηρ, "mother"). This makes him rewarding but demanding to read in Greek.
timeline: Born at Eleusis (525/4 BCE)
First competes at the City Dionysia, c. 499 BCE
Fights at Marathon
First victory at the Dionysia
Persians, the earliest securely dated surviving tragedy, wins first prize; the young Pericles pays for the production
Defeated by Sophocles in the younger poet's first victory (Plutarch, Cimon 8)
Seven against Thebes, the last play of a trilogy on the house of Laius
Oresteia (Agamemnon, Libation Bearers, Eumenides) wins first prize
Dies at Gela in Sicily (456/5 BCE); the story that an eagle dropped a tortoise on his head is a later anecdote
Lycurgus has official copies of the three tragedians' plays deposited in Athens, c. 330 BCE, to curb actors' alterations
Aldine editio princeps (Venice), which runs the surviving parts of Agamemnon and Libation Bearers together as one play
core.manuscripts:
Galen tells a story that Ptolemy III borrowed the official Athenian copies of the tragedians against a deposit of fifteen talents and simply kept them; whatever its truth, our texts descend from the editions of the Alexandrian scholars. After that almost everything depends on one book: the Medicean manuscript in Florence (Laurentianus 32.9, called M), copied in the late tenth century, which also contains Sophocles and Apollonius of Rhodes. For the Suppliants and the Libation Bearers it is the only independent witness, and it has lost the opening of the Libation Bearers, some of which is recovered from quotations in Aristophanes' Frogs.

M has also lost large parts of the Agamemnon (lines 311–1066, and from 1160 to the end). For those passages editors depend on manuscripts connected with the fourteenth-century edition of the Byzantine scholar Demetrius Triclinius: Laurentianus 31.8 (F), Marcianus gr. 616 in Venice (G), and Triclinius' own copy in Naples (T). Three plays, Prometheus, Seven against Thebes and Persians, were read in Byzantine schools as the 'Byzantine triad' and survive in many manuscripts, with Byzantine commentaries. The other four are much more thinly attested.
core.variants:
Aeschylus' text is among the most corrupt in Greek literature, and his choral lyrics in particular are full of passages that editors have had to repair by conjecture. Because M is missing so much of the Agamemnon, nearly half of that play rests on the Triclinian manuscripts alone, which all go back to a single late source.

Whether Prometheus Bound is really by Aeschylus has been questioned since the nineteenth century on grounds of metre, style and staging. Many scholars now doubt it, and some suggest that it was completed or staged after his death, perhaps by his son Euphorion, but the question is still open. The end of the Seven against Thebes, where Antigone resolves to bury her brother against the city's decree (1005–78), is widely thought to have been added later, probably under the influence of Sophocles' Antigone. After Aeschylus' death Athens allowed his plays to be restaged, and actors' changes in these revivals are one reason Lycurgus had an official text made.

core.summary:
Alexander of Aphrodisias (Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Ἀφροδισιεύς, Alexandros ho Aphrodisieus, fl. c. 200 CE) was the most important ancient commentator on Aristotle, called by later writers simply 'the Commentator' (ὁ ἐξηγητής, ho exēgētēs). He came from Aphrodisias in Caria, where an inscription honouring his father, also a philosopher, has been found. In the dedication of his treatise On Fate he thanks the emperors Septimius Severus and Caracalla for appointing him to a chair of Aristotelian philosophy, probably at Athens, between 198 and 209.

His commentaries survive on the first books of the Metaphysics, the first book of the Prior Analytics, the Topics, the Meteorology and On Sense and Sensibles. He also wrote independent treatises: On the Soul, which developed an influential theory of the intellect; On Fate, a defence of human responsibility against Stoic determinism; On Mixture; and several collections of short Questions. His interpretations shaped the reading of Aristotle for more than a thousand years, among Greek Neoplatonists, Arabic philosophers such as al-Farabi and Averroes, and Latin scholastics.

Alexander's Greek is the precise, economical prose of the philosophical schools, closely following Aristotle's terminology. It rewards readers who already know Aristotle.
timeline: Appointed to a chair of Aristotelian philosophy by Septimius Severus and Caracalla (198–209)
Writes his commentaries and treatises, including On Fate (c. 200)
Many of his works are translated into Arabic (9th century)
Commentaria in Aristotelem Graeca publishes his commentaries (from 1891)
core.manuscripts: Each of Alexander's works has its own tradition, and several survive in only one or two Greek manuscripts. Some works lost in Greek survive in Arabic or Latin translations, and the Arabic versions are important for his theory of the intellect.
core.variants: A number of works under his name are not his, including the commentary on the later books of the Metaphysics (probably by the Byzantine scholar Michael of Ephesus), the commentary on the Sophistical Refutations, the Ethical Problems and the treatise On Fevers. The Mantissa and the Questions are collections of short pieces, and scholars debate which of them come from Alexander and which from his school.

core.summary:
Andocides (Ἀνδοκίδης, Andokidēs, c. 440–after 391 BCE) was an Athenian aristocrat whose life was shaped by a single scandal. In 415, as the great expedition to Sicily was about to sail, the herms, sacred pillars that stood throughout the city, were mutilated in one night, and the Eleusinian Mysteries were said to have been profaned in private houses. Andocides was arrested and, to save himself and his family, gave information naming others, in exchange for immunity. A decree barring those guilty of impiety from the temples and the marketplace drove him into exile, and he spent years as a merchant around the Aegean.

He returned under the amnesty of 403. His speech On the Mysteries (400/399), his defence when his enemies tried to prosecute him for impiety again, is a vivid, first-hand account of the scandal of 415 and of Athenian law after the restoration of democracy; he was acquitted. On His Return is an earlier, unsuccessful plea to be allowed home. On the Peace with Sparta (392/1) urged the Athenians to accept a treaty he had helped negotiate; its rejection sent him into exile again, and nothing is known of him afterwards. A fourth speech in the collection, Against Alcibiades, is a later rhetorical exercise.

Andocides was an amateur, not a professional speechwriter, and ancient critics ranked him low among the ten Attic orators. His Greek is plain and conversational, sometimes loose in construction, but his narrative is lively and personal, and he is an important historical source.
timeline: Born in Athens to an aristocratic family (c. 440)
Mutilation of the herms and profanation of the Mysteries; Andocides informs to save himself
On His Return, an unsuccessful plea to come home (c. 410–405)
Returns to Athens under the amnesty
On the Mysteries (400/399); acquitted
On the Peace with Sparta (392/1); exiled again

core.manuscripts: Andocides survives mainly in the early fourteenth-century Codex Crippsianus in the British Library (Burney 95, A), the most important manuscript of the minor Attic orators, and in manuscripts related to it. The Crippsianus was copied at Constantinople by a known scribe, Michael Klostomalles.
core.variants: The text depends on a narrow tradition, so many corruptions have to be corrected by conjecture. The authenticity of Against Alcibiades has long been rejected; it presents itself as a speech of 415 but is generally regarded as a later composition. The documents quoted in On the Mysteries may include later insertions, though some are probably genuine.
editions: K. J. Maidment, Minor Attic Orators I: Antiphon, Andocides (Loeb Classical Library, 1941) — the Greek text and translation used here

core.summary:
Anna Komnene (Ἄννα Κομνηνή, Anna Komnēnē, 1083–c. 1153) was the eldest child of the emperor Alexios I Komnenos. She was born 'in the purple' (πορφυρογέννητος, porphyrogennētos), in the palace chamber reserved for imperial births, and received an exceptional education in literature, philosophy and medicine. She married the soldier and historian Nikephoros Bryennios. After her father's death in 1118 she was implicated in a failed plot against her brother, John II, and spent her later years in the convent of the Theotokos Kecharitomene in Constantinople, which her mother had founded.

The Alexiad (Ἀλεξιάς), in fifteen books, completed around 1148, is a history of her father's life and reign (1081–1118), begun, she says, to complete the unfinished work of her husband. It describes Alexios' wars against the Normans, Pechenegs and Seljuk Turks, and it is our only Byzantine account of the First Crusade by an eyewitness of its arrival in Constantinople. Anna writes as a devoted daughter, and her portrait of her father is openly admiring; she is sharp about the crusaders and the Normans.

Her Greek is a learned, Atticising literary language far removed from the Greek spoken in her day, full of quotations from Homer and allusions to classical authors. She often apologises for having to use barbarous foreign names and calls the western crusaders by the ancient name Κελτοί (Keltoi, "Celts"). The Alexiad is one of the landmarks of Byzantine literature and one of the few major historical works by a woman before modern times.
timeline: Her father Alexios I Komnenos becomes emperor
Born in the Porphyra of the palace at Constantinople (1 December 1083)

core.manuscripts: The Alexiad survives in a small number of manuscripts. The most important are two of the twelfth century: Coislinianus 311 in Paris and Laurentianus 70.2 in Florence. There is also an abridgement made in the thirteenth century. Some leaves are lost, so there are gaps in the narrative.
core.variants: Scholars debate how far the Alexiad is Anna's own work, how much it draws on the notes and memoirs of her husband and of veterans of her father's campaigns, and when its parts were written. A minority view assigns much of it to Bryennios' materials; most scholars treat Anna as a genuine and highly personal author. Her chronology is sometimes confused.

core.summary:
Antiphon of Rhamnus (Ἀντιφῶν, Antiphōn, c. 480–411 BCE) was the first Athenian to write speeches for others to deliver in court and to publish them, and later tradition made him the teacher of Thucydides. Thucydides himself describes him as the brains behind the oligarchic coup of 411 that set up the regime of the Four Hundred: a man second to none in ability, who preferred to work behind the scenes. When the oligarchy fell, Antiphon was tried for treason and executed. Thucydides calls his defence speech the finest ever made by a man on trial for his life, and papyrus fragments of it survive.

Three of his court speeches survive: Against the Stepmother, a son's prosecution of his stepmother for poisoning his father; On the Murder of Herodes; and On the Choreutes, about a boy who died while training for a festival chorus. Three Tetralogies, sets of four model speeches (two for each side) on imaginary homicide cases, show how arguments from probability could be built on both sides. Their authorship is disputed. Whether this Antiphon is the same man as Antiphon the Sophist, whose philosophical fragments are listed separately, is also debated.

Antiphon's Greek is austere and old-fashioned, with the -σσ- spellings of older Attic (θάλασσα, not θάλαττα), poetic words and heavy, formal antitheses. He is the earliest Attic prose writer whose speeches survive, and his work shows Athenian rhetoric in the making.
timeline: Born at Rhamnus in Attica (c. 480)
Active as a teacher of rhetoric and the first professional speechwriter

core.manuscripts: The speeches survive mainly in the early fourteenth-century Codex Crippsianus in the British Library (Burney 95, A) and related manuscripts. Papyrus fragments of his defence speech of 411 (On the Revolution) and of works attributed to Antiphon the Sophist come from Egypt.
core.variants: The chief questions are ones of authorship. The Tetralogies contain features of language and law that some scholars think un-Athenian or later, and others defend as Antiphon's. There has been a long debate over whether the orator and the sophist are one person or two. Most scholars now incline to two, though the question is open.

core.summary:
Apollonius of Rhodes (Ἀπολλώνιος Ῥόδιος, Apollōnios Rhodios, 3rd century BCE) was an Alexandrian scholar and poet. An ancient list of the heads of the Library of Alexandria places him between Zenodotus and Eratosthenes, and he is said to have tutored the future Ptolemy III. His ancient Lives say that he was a pupil of Callimachus, that an early recital of his poem failed, and that he withdrew to Rhodes, which gave him his name. Much of this looks like later storytelling, including the tale of a bitter quarrel with Callimachus.

His Argonautica (Ἀργοναυτικά), in four books of about 5,800 lines, is the only Greek epic to survive from the long gap between Homer and the Roman empire. It tells how Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis for the Golden Fleece and back. Its heart is Book 3, where Medea falls in love with Jason and betrays her father to help him. This is one of the first great studies of love in European literature, and Virgil drew on it for Dido in the Aeneid. Apollonius' Jason is an uncertain, modern sort of hero, and the poem is full of learned explanations of places, cults and customs.

Apollonius writes in Homer's language, but not as Homer did. He uses rare Homeric words in carefully chosen new senses, reshapes formulas, and avoids the repetitions of oral epic. The poem opens with an address to Apollo: Ἀρχόμενος σέο, Φοῖβε, παλαιγενέων κλέα φωτῶν / μνήσομαι (Archomenos seo, Phoibe, palaigeneōn klea phōtōn / mnēsomai, "Beginning with you, Phoebus, I will recall the famous deeds of men of old").
timeline: Born, perhaps c. 295 BCE; ancient sources call him Alexandrian or Naucratite
Head of the Library of Alexandria after Zenodotus (date uncertain)

core.manuscripts: The chief manuscript is the same tenth-century Florentine codex that preserves Aeschylus and Sophocles, Laurentianus 32.9 (L). The other medieval manuscripts, mostly of the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, form a few related groups. The poem comes with a large body of ancient commentary (scholia), which a note in L says was drawn from the commentaries of Lucillus of Tarrha, Sophocleus and Theon. It preserves much learned information on myth and geography. Papyri of the Roman period add early evidence.
core.variants: The scholia quote readings from an 'earlier edition' (προέκδοσις, proekdosis) of Book 1 that differ from our text, which suggests that Apollonius revised his poem, or that ancient scholars believed he had. Otherwise the text is fairly sound. Editors disagree mainly over Homeric forms, which scribes tended to normalize, and over some obscure geographical passages in Book 4.

core.summary:
Appian (Ἀππιανός, Appianos, c. 95–c. 165 CE) was a Greek of Alexandria, where he lived through the Jewish revolt of 115–117. He moved to Rome, practised as an advocate, and became a Roman citizen. His friend Fronto, the tutor of Marcus Aurelius, wrote to the emperor Antoninus Pius (between 147 and 161) asking that the elderly Appian be given the honorary rank of procurator. The preface to his history describes his career.

His Roman History (Ῥωμαϊκά, Rhōmaika), in twenty-four books, was arranged not by date but by region: each book tells the story of Rome's wars with one people or area, from the kings and the conquest of Italy to Spain, Carthage, Macedonia, Syria and Mithridates, followed by five books on the Civil Wars from the Gracchi (133 BCE) to 35 BCE. The books on Spain, Hannibal, Carthage, Illyria, Syria, Mithridates and the Civil Wars survive; the others are known from excerpts. The Civil Wars are our only continuous ancient narrative of the Roman revolution, and an English translation of 1578 was probably among Shakespeare's sources for Julius Caesar.

Appian writes plain, clear Koine, with little rhetorical ornament. He is interested in why Rome came to rule the world and in the dangers of civil strife, and he relies heavily on earlier sources, now lost, which makes him valuable even where he is uncritical.
timeline: Born at Alexandria (c. 95)

core.manuscripts: The surviving books come down in a limited number of medieval manuscripts, and each group of books has its own tradition. The lost books survive mainly through excerpts made for the emperor Constantine VII and through summaries by Photius, who read the complete work.
core.variants: Appian's accounts sometimes contradict other sources because he compresses and rearranges material from several predecessors, and his chronology can be confused. Scholars debate which lost historians he followed, especially for the Civil Wars. The book called Parthian Wars in older editions is not by Appian but a later compilation from Plutarch.

core.summary:
Aratus of Soli (Ἄρατος, Aratos, c. 315–c. 240 BCE) came from Cilicia, studied in Athens, where he came to know the Stoic Zeno, and in about 276 was invited to the court of King Antigonus Gonatas at Pella in Macedonia. There he wrote the Phaenomena (Φαινόμενα, "Appearances"), a poem of 1,154 hexameters that sets out in verse the constellations described in prose by the astronomer Eudoxus, followed by a section on weather signs.

The poem opens with a hymn to Zeus, Ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα (Ek Dios archōmestha, "Let us begin from Zeus"), and a phrase from its fifth line, "for we are also his offspring", is quoted by Paul in his speech at Athens (Acts 17:28). Callimachus praised Aratus' refined art, and he hid in his description of the crescent moon an acrostic, in which the first letters of lines 783–787 spell ΛΕΠΤΗ (leptē, "slender, refined"), the watchword of the new poetics. The Phaenomena became one of the most widely read poems of antiquity. It was translated into Latin by Cicero, Germanicus and Avienus, commented on by the astronomer Hipparchus, and copied throughout the Middle Ages.

Aratus writes in Homeric and Hesiodic language, polished and allusive, with a Stoic vision of a universe ordered by Zeus for the good of mankind.

core.manuscripts: The Phaenomena survives in many medieval manuscripts, often with extensive ancient commentaries (scholia) and illustrations of the constellations. The poem was part of the basic education in astronomy in Byzantium and was copied very widely.
core.variants: The text is generally sound. The main problems concern the scholia and the ancient Lives of Aratus, which are contradictory. Scholars also discuss the relation between the poem's astronomy, which follows Eudoxus closely, and the actual sky of Aratus' day, as Hipparchus already noted.

core.summary:
Archimedes of Syracuse (Ἀρχιμήδης, Archimēdēs, c. 287–212 BCE) was the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He was the son of an astronomer, Phidias, and according to Plutarch a friend and perhaps a relative of King Hieron II. He sent his discoveries as letters to mathematicians at Alexandria, among them Conon, Dositheus and Eratosthenes. During the Roman siege of Syracuse (214–212) his war machines held off the attackers for many months, and he was killed when the city fell. Cicero, as quaestor in Sicily, found his neglected tomb, marked as he had wished with a sphere inside a cylinder. The story of "Eureka!" in the bath comes from Vitruvius, two centuries later.

His surviving works include On the Sphere and Cylinder, which proves that a sphere has two-thirds the volume of its circumscribing cylinder, Measurement of a Circle (with its famous bounds for π), On Spirals, On Plane Equilibria, On Floating Bodies and The Sand-Reckoner. In the Sand-Reckoner he builds a number system large enough to count the grains of sand that would fill the universe, and reports Aristarchus' theory that the earth moves round the sun. The Method, in which he explains how he found results by imagined weighing before proving them rigorously, was lost until the twentieth century.

Archimedes wrote in his native Doric, the dialect of Syracuse, though later copyists turned much of it into the standard Koine of mathematics. His proofs are demanding, using a rigorous method of exhaustion and double reductio ad absurdum, but his prefaces, addressed to friends, are personal and lively.

Killed when Syracuse falls to Marcellus

core.manuscripts: Three Byzantine manuscripts carried Archimedes to the Renaissance, and only one survives. Codex A, owned by the humanist Giorgio Valla, was lost in the sixteenth century after many copies had been made from it. Codex B, used by William of Moerbeke for his Latin translation of 1269, was lost soon after. Codex C, copied around 950, was scraped in 1229 and its leaves reused for a prayer book. J. L. Heiberg identified the faint lower text in 1906. This Archimedes Palimpsest is our only source for the Method and the Stomachion and for the Greek of On Floating Bodies, and modern multispectral imaging has recovered much of it.
core.variants: Because A is lost, its text must be reconstructed from its Renaissance copies, from Moerbeke's Latin and, where it overlaps, from the palimpsest. The copyists' conversion of Archimedes' Doric into Koine means that editors must decide how far to restore his dialect. Some works in the collection are not by Archimedes in their present form: the Book of Lemmas (Liber assumptorum) survives only through an Arabic version, and the Cattle Problem is a verse puzzle attributed to him.

core.summary:
Aelius Aristides (Αἴλιος Ἀριστείδης, Ailios Aristeidēs, 117–after 180 CE) was born into a wealthy family at Hadrianoi in Mysia, in north-western Asia Minor, and trained as an orator at Smyrna and Athens. In 143/4, on a journey to Rome, he fell seriously ill. For the rest of his life he suffered from a series of illnesses and spent long periods at the sanctuary of the healing god Asclepius at Pergamum. His Sacred Tales (Ἱεροὶ λόγοι, Hieroi logoi), begun around 171, record the dreams, treatments and revelations he received from the god. They are one of the most personal documents of ancient religion.

Aristides was the most admired orator of his age and, for Byzantine readers, a classic second only to Demosthenes. His speech To Rome (Oration 26) is the fullest praise of the Roman empire written by a Greek, and his Panathenaic Oration (1) celebrates the history and culture of Athens. When Smyrna was destroyed by an earthquake in 177, his appeal to Marcus Aurelius helped win imperial help for its rebuilding, and Philostratus wrote that it was no exaggeration to call Aristides Smyrna's founder. Other speeches defend oratory against Plato's attacks in the Gorgias, or were written for festivals and cities.

His Greek is strict, polished Attic, with long, elaborately balanced periods in the manner of Demosthenes and Plato. Its richness makes him demanding, but he was a model of style throughout the Byzantine centuries.
timeline: Born at Hadrianoi in Mysia (26 November 117)
Falls seriously ill on a journey to Rome (143/4)
Begins long stays at the Asclepieion of Pergamum

core.manuscripts: Aristides was a school author in Byzantium and survives in a very large number of manuscripts, many with scholia. The corpus is divided into several groups of speeches with different traditions, and some manuscripts go back to the tenth century. A few speeches under his name, such as the Art of Rhetoric, are not his.
core.variants: The numbering of the speeches differs between the old edition of Dindorf and the modern ones of Keil and of Lenz and Behr, so references need care. The authenticity of a few speeches, including some addressed to cities, is disputed. The Art of Rhetoric printed in Spengel's Rhetores Graeci is spurious.

core.summary:
Aristophanes (Ἀριστοφάνης, Aristophanēs, c. 446–c. 386 BCE) is the only poet of Athenian Old Comedy whose plays survive whole. He wrote about forty comedies, and eleven survive, from the Acharnians (425 BCE) to Wealth (388 BCE). His first plays were produced through other men, and his attack on the demagogue Cleon in the lost Babylonians (426) led Cleon to denounce him before the Council. Plato gives him a memorable speech in the Symposium: the myth of the split humans who spend their lives looking for their other halves.

Old Comedy was a public, political art. Aristophanes' plays mix fantastic plots (a private peace treaty, a city in the clouds built by birds, a sex strike to end the war, a journey to the underworld to bring back a tragedian) with personal abuse of living Athenians, obscenity, parody of tragedy, and choral lyric of real beauty. At the centre of most plays stands the parabasis (παράβασις, parabasis, "stepping forward"), where the chorus turns to address the audience directly, often in the poet's own voice. The Clouds' portrait of Socrates as a sophist and star-gazer is one of the prejudices Plato's Socrates says he must answer at his trial (Apology 19c).

His Greek is the living Attic of the Athenian street, turned in an instant into mock-tragic grandeur or lyric. He coins words freely: the birds' city is Νεφελοκοκκυγία (Nephelokokkygia, "Cloudcuckooland", Birds 819), and the frogs sing βρεκεκεκὲξ κοὰξ κοάξ (brekekekex koax koax, Frogs 209). The constant jokes about contemporaries make a commentary essential, and the rewards are great.
timeline: Born in Athens (c. 446 BCE), of the deme Cydathenaeum

Babylonians (lost); Cleon denounces him before the Council

core.manuscripts:
All eleven plays survive together in only one medieval manuscript, the Ravenna codex (Ravennas 429, R, mid-tenth century). It is also our only medieval witness for Women at the Thesmophoria and for about a quarter of Lysistrata. The Venetus (Marcianus gr. 474, V, eleventh or twelfth century) contains seven plays. Wealth, Clouds and Frogs formed the Byzantine school 'triad' and survive in a great many copies.

The plays come with rich ancient commentaries (scholia), which go back to Alexandrian scholarship and to later commentators such as Didymus and Symmachus. Papyri add fragments of the lost plays.
core.variants: Many of the problems are practical. Ancient copies marked a change of speaker only with a dash or a double point, so editors must decide who says which line, and editions often differ. The Clouds we have is a partial revision of the play that failed in 423; an ancient summary (hypothesis) says the revision was never finished, which explains some inconsistencies. Several dates and prizes are known only from these summaries. Nearly a thousand fragments of the lost plays survive in quotations and papyri.

core.summary:
Aristotle (Ἀριστοτέλης, Aristotelēs, 384–322 BCE) came from Stagira in Chalcidice, in northern Greece; his father Nicomachus was physician to the king of Macedon. He studied and taught in Plato's Academy for twenty years, served as tutor to the young Alexander the Great, and then taught at Athens in the Lyceum, a public gymnasium, where his school (later called the Peripatetic) took shape. Few thinkers have ranged so widely. He wrote on logic, physics, biology, the soul, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetry, and in many of these fields his work was the starting point for everyone who came after.

What survives is mostly his teaching material: compressed, technical treatises written for use in the school. The polished dialogues that ancient readers admired, and that Cicero praised for their "golden stream of speech", are lost except for fragments. His Greek can therefore feel abrupt, but it is precise, and he builds technical terms out of ordinary words: τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι (to ti ēn einai, literally "the what-it-was-to-be") is his phrase for a thing's essence. His vocabulary, ἐνέργεια (energeia, "activity, actuality"), οὐσία (ousia, "being, substance"), τέλος (telos, "end, goal") and many more, became the working language of philosophy for two thousand years, first in Greek and then, through Syriac, Arabic and Latin translations, across the medieval world.
timeline: Born at Stagira in Chalcidice
Enters Plato's Academy at seventeen
Leaves Athens around the time of Plato's death; years at Assos and on Lesbos, where much of his biological research was done
Tutor to Alexander at the Macedonian court

Dies at Chalcis

core.manuscripts:
According to Strabo and Plutarch, Aristotle's own library passed to his successor Theophrastus and then to Neleus of Scepsis, whose heirs hid it in a cellar; it was rediscovered in the first century BCE and taken to Rome by Sulla. There Andronicus of Rhodes edited the school treatises and gave the corpus the shape it still has. The story is dramatic and probably simplified: some of the treatises were known in the Hellenistic period, and another tradition says Neleus sold his books to the library at Alexandria.

Over a thousand medieval manuscripts of Aristotle survive, the oldest from the ninth and tenth centuries. For the Nicomachean Ethics, the work most readers start with, the main witnesses are a tenth-century manuscript in Florence (Laurentianus 81.11, Kb), a twelfth-century one in Paris (Parisinus gr. 1854, Lb) and a fifteenth-century one in Venice (Marcianus gr. 213, Mb). Robert Grosseteste's Latin translation (around 1246) is also valuable, because it was made from a Greek manuscript older than most of those that survive. The Poetics hangs by a thinner thread: one Greek manuscript of the tenth or eleventh century (Parisinus gr. 1741), a second, later one, William of Moerbeke's Latin translation (1278) and a tenth-century Arabic version made from a Syriac one, which is included in this collection.
core.variants:
Three books of the Nicomachean Ethics (5–7) are word for word the same as three books of the Eudemian Ethics (4–6), and scholars still disagree about which work they first belonged to. The Nicomachean Ethics also discusses pleasure twice, in 7.11–14 and again in 10.1–5, which some take as a sign that it combines separate courses of lectures. The Constitution of the Athenians, a work of Aristotle's school whether or not he wrote it himself, was lost until a papyrus copy was identified in the British Museum in 1890.

Not everything under Aristotle's name is his. Among the works in this collection, the Mechanica, Problemata, Physiognomonica, De coloribus, De audibilibus, Mirabilium auscultationes, Economics, the Letters and the Divisiones are generally regarded as the work of his school or of later writers, and the Magna Moralia is disputed. The Greek De plantis is a curiosity: it is a medieval translation back into Greek of a Latin version, itself made from Arabic, of a work by Nicolaus of Damascus. Bekker's Berlin edition has long been superseded as a text, but its page, column and line numbers (such as 1094a1, the opening of the Nicomachean Ethics) are still how every passage of Aristotle is cited.

core.summary:
Arrian (Ἀρριανός, Arrianos; Lucius Flavius Arrianus, c. 86/89–after 145/6 CE) came from a leading family of Nicomedia in Bithynia and had a full Roman career. As a young man he studied with Epictetus at Nicopolis and took down his lectures. He entered the Roman senate, was consul around 130, and governed Cappadocia for Hadrian from about 131 to 137, where he drove back an invasion of the Alans. Late in life he lived in Athens, where he was archon in 145/6.

His Anabasis of Alexander (Ἀλεξάνδρου ἀνάβασις), in seven books, is the best surviving account of Alexander's campaigns. In the preface Arrian explains that he follows Ptolemy and Aristobulus, two officers who marched with Alexander, and that he adds other stories only as 'what is said' (λεγόμενα, legomena). His Indica, a companion piece, describes India and Nearchus' voyage home. He also published the Discourses of Epictetus and the Handbook, and wrote on hunting, tactics and a coastal survey of the Black Sea addressed to Hadrian. His histories of Alexander's successors, of Bithynia and of Parthia are lost.

Arrian modelled himself on Xenophon, whom he admired as soldier, philosopher and historian; the title Anabasis echoes Xenophon's, and his own writings call him a "new Xenophon". His Greek is clear Atticising prose in Xenophon's manner. The Indica, by contrast, is written in Ionic in imitation of Herodotus.

Suffect consul at Rome (c. 129/130)
Governor of Cappadocia (c. 131–137); writes the Periplus of the Black Sea for Hadrian

Dies, some time after 145/6 (perhaps c. 160)

core.manuscripts: All manuscripts of the Anabasis and the Indica descend from a single codex in Vienna (Vindobonensis hist. gr. 4, A, c. 1200), as A. G. Roos showed in 1904. It was damaged by damp in the fifteenth century, and leaves carrying part of the beginning of the Anabasis and the end of the Indica were lost; they survive only in copies made before the damage. There is also a gap in Book 7 of the Anabasis. The shorter works have separate traditions.
core.variants: With one surviving archetype, gaps and corruptions in the Anabasis can be repaired only by conjecture or from the copies of A made before it was damaged. The lacuna in Book 7 has swallowed part of the narrative of Alexander's last months. Some shorter works under Arrian's name, such as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, are not his (see Pseudo-Arrianus).

core.summary:
Athanasius of Alexandria (Ἀθανάσιος, Athanasios, c. 296–373 CE) attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 as a deacon and secretary to his bishop, Alexander, and succeeded him as bishop of Alexandria in 328. For the next forty-five years he was the leading champion of the Nicene creed against Arius and his followers, who held that the Son was a created being. His opponents were powerful, and he was exiled five times, under Constantine, Constantius II, Julian and Valens, spending some seventeen years away from his see, at one point hidden among the monks of the Egyptian desert.

His early double treatise Against the Pagans and On the Incarnation of the Word explains why God became man. The Orations against the Arians (the fourth, included here, is not his) and On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea defend the Nicene faith. His Life of Antony, the story of the Egyptian hermit, became one of the most influential books of the Christian world and a model for all later saints' lives. His Festal Letter of 367 is the first surviving list of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.

Athanasius writes a clear, direct Greek, forceful in argument and sparing in rhetoric. On the Incarnation is short, accessible and a good introduction to the theological language of the fourth century.

core.manuscripts: Athanasius' works survive in many manuscripts, gathered into several ancient and Byzantine collections that differ in content and order. Some works were preserved because they were included in collections of documents on the Arian controversy. Many works falsely attributed to him also circulated under his name.
core.variants: The date of Against the Pagans and On the Incarnation is disputed, some placing it before 325 and others in the 330s. The fourth Oration against the Arians and many smaller works in the corpus are not his. The documents he quotes in his apologetic works raise questions of their own, since he selected them to support his case.

core.summary:
Athenaeus of Naucratis (Ἀθήναιος, Athēnaios, fl. c. 200 CE) came from a Greek city in the Nile Delta and lived in Rome. His one surviving work, the Deipnosophistae (Δειπνοσοφισταί, Deipnosophistai, "The Learned Banqueters"), was written soon after the death of Commodus in 192. It survives in fifteen books, some only in an abridged form.

The work describes a series of dinners given by a wealthy Roman, Larensis, for a company of scholars, poets, philosophers, lawyers and doctors, among them a character named Galen. The guests discuss everything that appears at a Greek banquet: fish, bread, wine, cups, cooks, music, dancing, courtesans, parasites and luxury. Every point is supported by quotations from earlier literature. Athenaeus quotes more than a thousand authors and many thousands of lines of verse, most of them from works now lost, especially Middle and New Comedy, and his book is one of the richest quarries for lost Greek literature and for daily life.

One of the guests, the grammarian Ulpian, questions every word to see whether it is attested in classical authors: "Is it found, or not?" (κεῖται ἢ οὐ κεῖται; keitai ē ou keitai?), which earned him the nickname Κειτούκειτος (Keitoukeitos). The joke captures the Atticising culture of the age. Athenaeus' own Greek is educated Koine with Attic polish, and the frame dialogue is light and often funny.
timeline: Death of Commodus, mentioned in the work as past

core.manuscripts: The full text survives in a single tenth-century manuscript in Venice, Marcianus gr. 447 (A), which has lost its beginning (the first two books and part of the third) and some other leaves. For those parts we depend on a Byzantine epitome of the whole work, preserved in several later manuscripts, which abridges and sometimes rewords the text.
core.variants: Where A is missing, the epitome gives only a shortened version, so the opening books are much less complete than the rest. The thousands of quotations raise their own problems: Athenaeus sometimes quotes from memory or from intermediate collections, and editors must decide whether a variant belongs to his source or to the transmission of his own text.

core.summary:
Bacchylides (Βακχυλίδης, Bakchylidēs, c. 518–c. 451 BCE) came from Iulis on the island of Ceos and was the nephew of the great lyric poet Simonides. Like Pindar, whose rival he was said to be, he composed victory odes and other choral songs for patrons across the Greek world, among them Hieron of Syracuse. For Hieron's chariot victory at Olympia in 468 it was Bacchylides, not Pindar, who wrote the celebration. The ancient scholars placed him among the nine canonical lyric poets.

For centuries almost nothing of his work survived. In 1896 the British Museum acquired from Egypt a papyrus roll with some fourteen victory odes and six dithyrambs, published by F. G. Kenyon in 1897. Among them are Ode 5, in which Heracles meets the ghost of Meleager in the underworld, and the dithyrambs about Theseus: Ode 17, where Theseus dives to the palace of Poseidon, and Ode 18, a dialogue between Aegeus and a chorus.

Bacchylides is clearer and more narrative than Pindar. He tells myths in vivid scenes, with rich descriptive compound adjectives and a literary Doric colouring (ᾱ for η). His poems are among the most accessible Greek lyric, and a good introduction to choral poetry.

Ode 3 celebrates Hieron's chariot victory at Olympia

core.manuscripts: Bacchylides has no medieval manuscript tradition. His text comes from the great London papyrus of the Roman period (P.Lond. 733), damaged in places, supplemented by smaller papyri and by quotations in later writers.
core.variants: The damage to the papyrus leaves many gaps that editors have filled by conjecture, and the order and numbering of some odes are uncertain. A few poems once attributed to him are now doubted. His birth date is uncertain; some scholars place it later than 518.

core.summary:
Basil of Caesarea (Βασίλειος, Basileios, c. 330–379 CE), called Basil the Great, came from a wealthy Christian family of Cappadocia that produced several saints, among them his sister Macrina and his brother Gregory of Nyssa. He studied at Constantinople and then at Athens, where his friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus began. After a short career as a teacher of rhetoric he turned to the ascetic life, visited monks in Egypt and Syria, and founded a community on his family's estate in Pontus. He became bishop of Caesarea in 370. As bishop he defended the Nicene faith against the emperor Valens and built outside the city a great complex for the poor and sick, known after him as the Basileias. He died, by tradition, on 1 January 379, though some scholars place his death in 377 or 378.

Basil's writings shaped Eastern Christianity. His rules for monks became the foundation of Greek monasticism, his treatise On the Holy Spirit helped settle the doctrine of the Trinity, and his homilies on the six days of creation (Hexaemeron) blend scripture with Greek natural science. More than three hundred of his letters survive, a vivid picture of a bishop's life in the fourth century. His short Address to Young Men on the Value of Greek Literature, included here, argues that Christians should read the pagan poets and philosophers, taking what is good from them as bees take honey from flowers. It was one of the most widely read Greek texts of the Renaissance.

Basil was trained in classical rhetoric, and his Greek is polished, Atticising prose, full of echoes of Plato and Plutarch. His letters range from formal treatises to warm notes to friends. Together with Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa he is one of the 'Cappadocian Fathers'.

core.manuscripts: Basil's works survive in a great many manuscripts. The letters come down in several ancient collections, arranged differently, so their order and numbering vary between editions. Some letters under his name, including parts of his supposed correspondence with the pagan rhetorician Libanius, are of doubtful authenticity. The Address to Young Men was copied, printed and translated more often than almost any other patristic text.
core.variants: The chief problems concern authenticity: several works and letters transmitted under Basil's name are now attributed to others, including some letters that are probably by his brother Gregory of Nyssa. The chronology of the letters, on which the story of his episcopate depends, is also disputed, as is the year of his death.

core.summary:
Callimachus (Καλλίμαχος, Kallimachos, c. 305–c. 240 BCE) came from Cyrene in North Africa and spent his career at Alexandria under Ptolemy II and Ptolemy III. He was the leading poet and one of the leading scholars of the new Hellenistic world. His Pinakes (Πίνακες, "Tables"), a catalogue of Greek literature in 120 books based on the holdings of the Library, made him the founder of Greek bibliography, although the ancient list of the Library's heads does not include him.

Only six hymns and some sixty epigrams came down through the Middle Ages. Everything else is known from papyri and quotations. That includes his most admired work, the Aetia (Αἴτια, "Causes"), four books of elegiac poems on the origins of cults and customs, as well as the Iambi and the Hecale, a short epic in which Theseus shelters in the hut of a poor old woman. The last poem of the Aetia, the Lock of Berenice, is best known through Catullus' Latin version (poem 66).

Callimachus championed short, polished, learned poetry over long traditional epic. In the prologue to the Aetia Apollo tells him to keep his sacrificial victim fat but his Muse "slender" (λεπταλέην, leptaleēn), and an epigram begins "I hate the cyclic poem" (ἐχθαίρω τὸ ποίημα τὸ κυκλικόν, echthairō to poiēma to kyklikon). Roman poets took him as their model, from Catullus to Propertius, who called himself the "Roman Callimachus", and Ovid. His Greek is dense with learning: rare words, Homeric glosses used in new senses, allusions to earlier poets, and a mix of dialects (the fifth and sixth hymns are in Doric). He wrote for readers who knew their Homer well, and he rewards slow reading.

core.manuscripts:
The Hymns survive because Byzantine scholars copied them in a collection of hymns together with the Homeric Hymns and the hymns of Orpheus and Proclus. The surviving manuscripts, mostly of the fifteenth century, go back to one lost archetype. The Epigrams survive mainly in the Greek Anthology.

For the rest we depend on papyri from Egypt, which over the last century have restored large parts of the Aetia, Iambi and Hecale. We also depend on quotations by later grammarians, and on a papyrus of prose summaries (the Milan Diegeseis) that outlines many of the lost poems.
core.variants: Because so much is fragmentary, the text of Callimachus is continually being rebuilt, and new papyri still change what we can read. Fragment numbers differ between editions (Pfeiffer, the Supplementum Hellenisticum, Harder's Aetia and others), so readers need to check which edition a reference uses. In the Hymns the main problems are dialect forms, which scribes normalized, and a few gaps. The dating of individual poems is much debated. So is the story of a bitter feud with Apollonius of Rhodes, which may be a later invention built on the Aetia prologue.

core.summary:
Cassius Dio (Κάσσιος Δίων, Kassios Diōn, c. 155–after 229 CE) came from a senatorial family of Nicaea in Bithynia. He entered the Roman senate under Commodus and held its highest offices: praetor in 194/5, consul around 205, and governor of Africa, Dalmatia and Upper Pannonia. In 229 he was consul for the second time, with the emperor Severus Alexander as his colleague, and then retired to Nicaea. He was an eyewitness of the reigns he describes from Commodus onwards.

His Roman History (Ῥωμαϊκὴ ἱστορία, Rhōmaikē historia), in eighty books, covered Rome from the arrival of Aeneas in Italy to his own consulship in 229. He tells us that he spent ten years gathering material and twelve writing. Books 36–60, covering 69 BCE to 46 CE, the fall of the Republic and the early Principate, survive largely complete. For the rest we depend on Byzantine epitomes, above all that of the monk John Xiphilinus (11th century) for Books 36–80 and the chronicle of Zonaras for the early books, and on excerpts. He is the most important source for the reign of Augustus and for the Severan emperors.

Dio wrote in a classicising Attic modelled on Thucydides, with set speeches that analyse political problems; the debate between Agrippa and Maecenas on monarchy and democracy (Book 52) is the most famous. His Greek is dense but regular, and it shows how a senator of the Greek East saw the Roman empire.

core.manuscripts: Books 36–60 survive in a handful of medieval manuscripts, the oldest from the tenth and eleventh centuries. For Books 78–79 we have a much older witness, the fifth- or sixth-century Vaticanus gr. 1288, damaged at beginning and end but preserving Dio's own text. Everything else depends on Xiphilinus' epitome, on Zonaras, and on the excerpts made for Constantine VII.
core.variants: Because the epitomators shortened, reworded and sometimes added to what they excerpted, it is often impossible to know Dio's exact words outside Books 36–60 and 78–79. Book numbers for the later part of the work differ between editions, which is why references are often given in the form 79(78). There are gaps within the surviving books, notably in Books 55–60.

core.summary:
Chariton (Χαρίτων, Charitōn, probably mid-1st century CE) introduces himself in the first sentence of his novel: "I, Chariton of Aphrodisias, secretary of the rhetor Athenagoras, will tell a love story that happened in Syracuse." Aphrodisias was a prosperous Greek city in Caria, in south-western Asia Minor. Nothing more is known of him. Most scholars now date him to the reign of Claudius or Nero, though some place him earlier.

His Callirhoe (Τὰ περὶ Χαιρέαν καὶ Καλλιρρόην, Ta peri Chairean kai Kallirrhoēn, "The Story of Chaereas and Callirhoe"), in eight books, is the earliest Greek novel to survive complete. Callirhoe, the beautiful daughter of the Syracusan general Hermocrates who defeated the Athenian expedition of 415–413 BCE, marries Chaereas. He strikes her in a fit of jealousy; she is buried alive and carried off by tomb robbers, and sold as a slave in Miletus, where she marries again. The story moves to the court of the Persian king at Babylon, through a trial and a war, to a happy reunion in Syracuse. The historical setting, the speeches and the scenes of public life give the novel the feel of historiography.

Chariton's Greek is simple and clear, closer to the educated Koine of his day than to the strict Attic of later novelists. He quotes Homer some thirty times at moments of high emotion, and his narrator often comments on events. A good reader for anyone who has finished a first year of Greek.

core.manuscripts: Callirhoe survives in a single medieval manuscript, the thirteenth-century Laurentianus Conventi Soppressi 627 in Florence (F), which is our only witness for about 95 per cent of the text. The same book contains Xenophon of Ephesus and Longus and part of Achilles Tatius. A few papyrus fragments of the second and third centuries CE and an early parchment codex confirm the text in places.
core.variants: With only one manuscript, errors must be corrected by conjecture, and there are small gaps. Scholars debate the date: a passage in the Roman satirist Persius (1.134) mentions a 'Callirhoe', which may or may not refer to this novel. The ending, in which Chariton addresses his readers directly, has been read as proof that he knew he was writing for a popular audience.

core.summary:
Chrysippus of Soli (Χρύσιππος, Chrysippos, c. 279–206 BCE) came to Athens from Cilicia, studied with the Stoic Cleanthes and in Plato's Academy, and succeeded Cleanthes as head of the Stoa around 230 BCE. He gave Stoicism its systematic form. Ancient readers said that "if there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa", and for later centuries 'the Stoic view' usually meant his view.

He was enormously productive: Diogenes Laertius credits him with more than 705 books. He was above all a logician, and his propositional logic, with its five 'indemonstrable' argument forms, is one of the great achievements of ancient philosophy; it was rediscovered and appreciated only in the twentieth century. He also wrote on physics, fate and providence, the soul and the passions, and ethics.

Not one of his works survives complete. We know him from quotations and reports in later writers, many of them critics: Plutarch, who wrote on the Stoics' self-contradictions; Galen, who attacked his theory of the soul; Diogenes Laertius; Cicero; and Sextus Empiricus. Charred papyri from Herculaneum preserve parts of his Logical Investigations. Ancient critics found his style careless and repetitive and mocked his habit of quoting poets at length. One joke ran that if you removed the quotations from one of his books, only blank papyrus would remain.

Comes to Athens; studies with Cleanthes and in the Academy
Succeeds Cleanthes as head of the Stoa (c. 230)
Dies at Athens (c. 206), reportedly aged 73

core.manuscripts: There is no manuscript tradition of Chrysippus. His words survive in quotations embedded in later authors, each transmitted in its own manuscripts, and in a few papyri from the library of the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum.
core.variants: The chief difficulty is deciding what Chrysippus actually said. Many reports come from hostile sources, such as Plutarch and Galen, who may quote selectively or paraphrase. Others do not distinguish him from Stoics in general. Von Arnim's collection arranges the fragments by topic, and some of his attributions are doubtful.

core.summary:
Claudius Ptolemy (Κλαύδιος Πτολεμαῖος, Klaudios Ptolemaios, c. 100–c. 170 CE) worked at Alexandria. The observations he records in his great astronomical work are dated between 127 and 141 CE, and almost nothing else is known of his life. His Latin family name shows that he was a Roman citizen; he wrote in Greek.

His Mathematical Syntaxis (Μαθηματικὴ σύνταξις, Mathēmatikē syntaxis), in thirteen books, set out a complete geometrical model of the motions of the sun, moon, planets and stars around a stationary earth, using eccentric circles, epicycles and the 'equant' point. Arab astronomers called it al-majisṭī ("the greatest"), which gave the Latin Almagest. It remained the foundation of astronomy until Copernicus, whose De revolutionibus (1543) followed its structure closely. Ptolemy also wrote the Tetrabiblos ("Four Books"), the standard ancient textbook of astrology, a Geography giving coordinates for some 8,000 places, and the Harmonics, a treatise on musical theory.

His Greek is the clear, technical prose of Hellenistic science. Numbers are written with the letters of the alphabet, and fractions in the Babylonian sexagesimal system, which is why we still divide degrees and hours into sixty minutes and sixty seconds. Readers will need a translation with notes for the mathematics, but the introductory chapters of the Almagest and the Tetrabiblos are approachable.

core.manuscripts: The Almagest survives in two important ninth-century manuscripts, Parisinus gr. 2389 (largely in capitals) and Vaticanus gr. 1594, the finest witness, rich in notes. J. L. Heiberg's edition was based on these and a few others. Arabic translations and the medieval Latin versions made from Arabic and from Greek are also important evidence. The Tetrabiblos, Geography and Harmonics each have separate traditions, and the Geography's maps and coordinate lists vary widely between manuscripts.
core.variants: In the Almagest the main problems are numerical: scribes miscopied the letter-numerals in the tables, and editors must check them against Ptolemy's own calculations. The coordinates of the Geography were revised and corrupted many times, so the maps drawn from them differ. Some works under his name, such as the Karpos (Centiloquium), a collection of astrological aphorisms, are not by him.

core.summary:
Clement of Alexandria (Κλήμης ὁ Ἀλεξανδρεύς, Klēmēs ho Alexandreus; Titus Flavius Clemens, c. 150–c. 215 CE) was probably born in Athens to a pagan family. After travelling in search of teachers he settled in Alexandria with the Christian teacher Pantaenus and became a leading teacher of the Christian community there. He left the city during the persecution of 202 and died some years later, perhaps in Asia Minor or Palestine.

Clement was the first Christian writer to engage fully with Greek philosophy and literature, arguing that philosophy had prepared the Greeks for Christ as the Law had prepared the Jews. His three main works form a sequence. The Protrepticus ("Exhortation to the Greeks") urges pagans to leave their myths and cults. The Paedagogus ("Tutor") teaches the convert how to live, down to food, dress and table manners. The Stromateis ("Patchwork" or "Miscellanies"), in eight books, is a deliberately loose collection of reflections on the true Christian 'gnostic'. He also wrote a sermon, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved?, and made excerpts from the Valentinian teacher Theodotus.

Clement writes a learned, ornate Greek and quotes hundreds of classical authors, poets, philosophers and historians, preserving many passages from lost works. The disputed Letter to Theodore, containing a 'Secret Gospel of Mark', was published by Morton Smith in 1973 from an eighteenth-century copy; its authenticity is still debated.

core.manuscripts: The Protrepticus and Paedagogus depend essentially on the Arethas codex (Parisinus gr. 451), copied in 913–914 for Arethas of Caesarea, the oldest collection of Christian apologetic writings. The Stromateis survive in a single eleventh-century manuscript in Florence (Laurentianus V 3), which may also have belonged to Arethas. The shorter works have separate traditions.
core.variants: Because the major works each rest on essentially one manuscript, many corruptions and gaps have to be repaired by conjecture. The Stromateis end abruptly, and the eighth book appears to be a collection of notes rather than a finished work. The authenticity of the Letter to Theodore is one of the most debated questions in early Christian studies.

core.summary:
Demosthenes (Δημοσθένης, Dēmosthenēs, 384–322 BCE) was the greatest orator of Athens; later antiquity called him simply ὁ ῥήτωρ (ho rhētōr, "the orator"), as Homer was "the poet". His father died when he was seven. He learned his craft, by tradition under the orator Isaeus, and first used it in lawsuits against the guardians who had squandered his inheritance. Plutarch, citing Demetrius of Phalerum, tells how he overcame a weak voice and an awkward delivery by practising with pebbles in his mouth, a story best taken as anecdote.

His great cause was resistance to Philip II of Macedon. In the Philippics and Olynthiacs he urged the Athenians to act before it was too late. After Philip defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, his rival Aeschines attacked a proposal to crown Demosthenes for his services. In reply Demosthenes defended his whole career in On the Crown (330 BCE), and Aeschines won so few votes that he left Athens. Ancient critics regarded the speech as his masterpiece. He died in 322, taking poison rather than fall into the hands of Macedonian soldiers.

His prose is tightly built, varied in rhythm and relentlessly argued. He avoids hiatus (a vowel at the end of one word meeting a vowel at the start of the next) and long runs of short syllables, and he can turn argument into oath. In On the Crown, defending the decision to fight at Chaeronea, he swears "No, by those of our ancestors who faced the danger at Marathon" (οὐ μὰ τοὺς Μαραθῶνι προκινδυνεύσαντας τῶν προγόνων, 18.208). He was the model for generations of orators; Cicero named his own speeches against Mark Antony Philippics after his.

core.manuscripts:
The text rests above all on a tenth-century manuscript in Paris (Parisinus gr. 2934, S), with three other early manuscripts: Marcianus gr. 416 in Venice (F), Monacensis gr. 485 in Munich (once at Augsburg and so called Augustanus, A) and Parisinus gr. 2935 (Y). S often lacks words and phrases that the others include. Whether these are later additions in the other manuscripts or omissions in S has long been argued, but since the nineteenth century editors have usually given S the greater weight.

Demosthenes became a school classic early, and many papyri of his speeches survive from Egypt, the earliest from the Ptolemaic period. One papyrus preserves part of a commentary on the Philippics by the Alexandrian scholar Didymus (first century BCE), a rare glimpse of ancient scholarship on the speeches.
core.variants: Not all of the 61 speeches in the collection are by Demosthenes. Several were written for or by others: Against Neaera and a group of other private speeches are the work of Apollodorus. The Fourth Philippic is doubted, On Halonnesus was attributed in antiquity to Hegesippus, and On the Treaty with Alexander, the Funeral Speech, the Erotic Essay and several of the Letters are widely considered spurious. The decrees and letters quoted in On the Crown were inserted later and are not genuine documents. The manuscript families also disagree over hundreds of small expansions to the text.

core.summary:
Dio of Prusa (Δίων, Diōn, c. 40–after 111 CE), later called Chrysostom (Χρυσόστομος, Chrysostomos, "golden-mouthed") for his eloquence, came from a leading family of Prusa in Bithynia. He began as a sophist and turned to philosophy under the Stoic Musonius Rufus. In the early 80s the emperor Domitian banished him from Rome, Italy and his homeland, and he spent years wandering in the dress of a Cynic philosopher, as far as the Greek cities on the northern Black Sea. Recalled by Nerva in 96, he returned to Prusa and public life; Pliny the Younger's letters to Trajan show him entangled around 111 in a dispute over a building project he had undertaken for his city.

Eighty speeches survive under his name, two of which (37 and 64) are now assigned to the sophist Favorinus. They range widely: four orations On Kingship addressed to Trajan; the Euboean Oration (7), which describes the simple life of a family of hunters and the problems of the urban poor; the Olympic Oration (12), on Phidias' statue of Zeus and how we come to know the gods; the Borysthenitic Oration (36), set in a Greek colony on the Black Sea; and the playful Trojan Oration (11), which argues that Troy was never taken. Many are addressed to the cities of Asia Minor, urging concord.

Dio's Greek is Atticising but clear and natural, modelled on Plato and Xenophon rather than on the more mannered sophists. His turn from rhetoric to philosophy became a famous story, told later by Synesius of Cyrene. He is a good author for readers who want imperial Greek prose that is elegant but not difficult.

Involved in a lawsuit over a building project at Prusa, reported by Pliny the Younger

core.manuscripts: The speeches survive in a good number of medieval manuscripts, which editors divide into families that differ in the number and order of the speeches. Some speeches are preserved in only one branch of the tradition.
core.variants: Besides the two speeches now given to Favorinus, a few others are of doubtful authenticity, and some appear to be drafts or fragments rather than finished works. The order and numbering of the speeches reflect later editors, not Dio. Dating individual speeches, especially those set during his exile, is often uncertain.

core.summary:
Diodorus of Sicily (Διόδωρος Σικελιώτης, Diodōros Sikeliōtēs, fl. c. 60–30 BCE) came from Agyrium in the interior of Sicily. He tells us that he visited Egypt in the 180th Olympiad (60–56 BCE), that he lived for many years in Rome, and that he spent thirty years on his history. The last events he mentions, among them Octavian's colony at Tauromenium in 36 BCE, show that he was still writing in the 30s.

His Library of History (Βιβλιοθήκη ἱστορική, Bibliothēkē historikē), in forty books, was a universal history from the mythical age to Caesar's wars in Gaul. Books 1–5 (the myths and early history of Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, Scythia, Arabia, North Africa and the Greeks) and Books 11–20 (Greek and Sicilian history from 480 to 302 BCE) survive complete. The rest are known from Byzantine excerpts and quotations. For much of the fourth century BCE, and for the wars of Alexander's successors, which he drew from the lost Hieronymus of Cardia, Diodorus is our only continuous narrative.

Diodorus has often been dismissed as a mere copyist of better historians such as Ephorus, Timaeus and Posidonius, and he does follow one source at a time. More recent scholarship stresses his own moral purpose and his vision of history as a single story of all humanity. His Greek is plain, serviceable Koine, easy to read and a good introduction to Hellenistic prose.
timeline: Born at Agyrium in Sicily (c. 90)
Visits Egypt during the 180th Olympiad (60–56 BCE)
Mentions Octavian's colony at Tauromenium, among the last events he records
Completes the Library of History (c. 30)
Excerpts from the lost books preserved in the collections made for Constantine VII (10th century)
Poggio Bracciolini's Latin translation of Books 1–5 printed at Bologna
Books 16–20 first printed in Greek at Basel
Henri Estienne prints all the surviving books
core.manuscripts: The two surviving blocks of the history, Books 1–5 and Books 11–20, reached the Middle Ages separately and have different manuscript traditions, the oldest witnesses dating from the tenth and eleventh centuries. The lost books survive only in fragments: excerpts made for the emperor Constantine VII, summaries by Photius, and quotations in later writers such as Eusebius, who used Diodorus for early history.
core.variants: Because Diodorus reproduces his sources closely, much scholarship has tried to identify which lost historian lies behind each section, and his own dates and numbers are often confused when he combines accounts. His chronology, which arranges events by Athenian archons and Roman consuls, contains many errors of a year or more. The text itself is fairly sound, but proper names are often corrupt.

K. S. Sacks, Diodorus Siculus and the First Century (Princeton, 1990)

core.summary:
Diogenes Laertius (Διογένης Λαέρτιος, Diogenēs Laertios), who probably lived in the first half of the third century CE, compiled the Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers in ten books. We know almost nothing about him beyond what the work reveals; at one point (3.47) he addresses a woman reader who "loves Plato". He arranges the philosophers in two lines of succession, an Ionian one that starts from Thales' pupil Anaximander and runs through Socrates and Plato, and an Italian one from Pythagoras, and ends with Epicurus. His work is a scrapbook more than a history: gossip, anecdotes, lists of books and witty sayings sit beside summaries of doctrine and some rather weak epigrams of his own.

It is nonetheless indispensable. Diogenes names more than two hundred earlier authors, most of them now lost, though he often knew them at second hand, and his work is our most important single source for the lives of the Greek philosophers. Book 10 quotes three letters of Epicurus, his will and his Principal Doctrines (Κύριαι δόξαι, Kyriai doxai) word for word, which makes it one of the main places where Epicurus survives in his own words.

His Greek is the plain prose of the imperial period and one of the easier texts for a reader moving on from a grammar. Much of it is built from chreiai, short anecdotes that end in a saying and follow a fixed pattern: ἐρωτηθεὶς … ἔφη (erōtētheis … ephē, "asked …, he said").
timeline: Approximate date of composition (the latest philosophers he mentions belong to the early third century)
Twelfth and thirteenth centuries: the three primary manuscripts (B, P, F) are copied
Ambrogio Traversari's Latin translation, finished about this year, circulates in Renaissance Italy
Editio princeps (Froben, Basel)
Marcus Meibom's edition introduces the section numbers still used for citation
core.manuscripts: Three medieval manuscripts are primary: one in Naples (B, twelfth century), one in Paris (Parisinus gr. 1759, P) and one in Florence (F, thirteenth century). All three go back to a single damaged ancestor. A Vatican manuscript (Vaticanus gr. 96) preserves an independent set of excerpts, and the Byzantine encyclopaedia known as the Suda draws on the work extensively.
core.variants: The text of Epicurus' letters in Book 10 is badly corrupted, and repairing it is central to the study of Epicureanism; the authenticity of one of them, the Letter to Pythocles, is also debated. Book 7, on the Stoics, breaks off in the middle of the life of Chrysippus; a table of contents preserved in one manuscript shows that the lost ending covered many more Stoics. The standard section numbers were introduced by Meibom in 1692.

core.summary:
Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Διονύσιος Ἁλικαρνασσεύς, Dionysios Halikarnasseus, c. 60–after 7 BCE) came to Rome in about 30 BCE, as Octavian ended the civil wars. He learned Latin, taught rhetoric to Roman and Greek pupils, and spent twenty-two years on his history, which he published in 7 BCE. He belonged to a circle of Greek and Roman intellectuals in Augustan Rome, and much of what we know of him comes from the letters and dedications in his own works.

His Roman Antiquities (Ῥωμαϊκὴ ἀρχαιολογία, Rhōmaikē archaiologia), in twenty books, told the history of Rome from its origins to the outbreak of the First Punic War in 264 BCE. Books 1–10 survive complete, Book 11 in part, and the rest in excerpts. Dionysius wanted to show Greek readers that the Romans were Greeks by origin and deserved their empire, and his work is, with Livy, our main source for early Rome.

He was also the leading literary critic of his age. His essays On the Ancient Orators, on Lysias, Isocrates, Isaeus, Demosthenes and Dinarchus, on Thucydides, and On the Arrangement of Words (De compositione verborum) analyse style with great precision, down to the sounds and rhythms of individual phrases. He championed a return to the Attic models of classical Athens against the florid 'Asianic' style, and his own Greek is careful, classicising Attic.
timeline: Born at Halicarnassus (c. 60)
Comes to Rome at the end of the civil wars (c. 30)
Writes his critical essays on the orators and on style (c. 30–10)
Publishes the first part of the Roman Antiquities
Excerpts from the lost books preserved in the collections made for Constantine VII (10th century)
Editio princeps of the Roman Antiquities (Paris, Robert Estienne)
core.manuscripts: The Roman Antiquities rest mainly on two groups of manuscripts, led by a tenth-century codex in the Chigi collection of the Vatican (Chisianus) and by Urbinas gr. 105 (tenth or eleventh century). A Byzantine epitome also survives. The critical essays have separate traditions. On the Arrangement of Words is found in the tenth- or eleventh-century Parisinus gr. 1741, the same manuscript that preserves Aristotle's Poetics and Rhetoric.
core.variants: The later books of the Roman Antiquities survive only in excerpts, and their placement is sometimes uncertain. Some works once attributed to Dionysius, notably an Art of Rhetoric, are not his. In the critical essays the many quotations from classical authors are an important secondary witness to their texts, and Dionysius' own text sometimes has to be corrected from the manuscripts of the authors he quotes.

core.summary:
Epictetus (Ἐπίκτητος, Epiktētos, c. 50–c. 135 CE) was born a slave at Hierapolis in Phrygia; his name simply means "acquired". His master in Rome was Epaphroditus, a freedman of Nero, who let him study with the Stoic Musonius Rufus. Once freed, he taught philosophy in Rome until the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Italy (c. 93). He then set up a school at Nicopolis in north-western Greece, where he taught for the rest of his life. He was lame, and later writers tell different stories about why.

Like Socrates, Epictetus wrote nothing. What we have comes from his pupil Arrian, later a Roman senator and the historian of Alexander, who took down his talks. Four books of Discourses (Διατριβαί, Diatribai) survive of an original eight, together with a short Handbook (Ἐγχειρίδιον, Encheiridion) of his main teachings. Their core is a single distinction, stated in the Handbook's first line: "Some things are up to us and some are not" (Τῶν ὄντων τὰ μέν ἐστιν ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν, τὰ δὲ οὐκ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν). Our judgements, desires and choices are ours; body, property, reputation and office are not, and freedom lies in caring only for what is ours to govern. Marcus Aurelius learned from these notes, Christian monks adapted the Handbook for their own use, and it has been read ever since.

Arrian says in his preface that he recorded Epictetus' words as nearly as possible as they were spoken, and it shows. This is the everyday Koine of the early empire: lively, blunt and full of imagined dialogue with a listener. Watch for the term προαίρεσις (prohairesis, "moral choice" or "will"), the one thing that, for Epictetus, no one can take from us.
timeline: Born a slave at Hierapolis in Phrygia (c. 50)
In Rome as the slave of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus; studies with Musonius Rufus
Domitian expels the philosophers from Italy; Epictetus opens his school at Nicopolis (c. 93)
Arrian studies with him and records his lectures (c. 108)
Dies at Nicopolis (c. 135)
Angelo Poliziano's Latin translation of the Handbook is printed, the first printed edition of any of his work
Editio princeps of the Discourses (Venice, Vittore Trincavelli), from a faulty manuscript
core.manuscripts: The surviving manuscripts of the Discourses all appear to descend from one book, an eleventh- or twelfth-century codex in the Bodleian Library at Oxford (Auct. T. 4. 13, S). Where it is damaged or wrong we have no independent check. The Handbook circulated much more widely and survives in many manuscripts, in Christian adaptations and in the sixth-century commentary of Simplicius. Fragments of the lost books come mainly from the anthology of Stobaeus.
core.variants: Because the Discourses depend on a single manuscript, their text has been repaired by conjecture in many places. The fragments attributed to Epictetus in Stobaeus and in later collections, such as the Gnomologium Epictetum included here, are of mixed authenticity, and some are certainly by others. How far Arrian polished what he heard, and so how close the Discourses are to a transcript, is still discussed.
