core.summary:
The New Testament (Ἡ Καινὴ Διαθήκη, Hē Kainē Diathēkē) is a collection of 27 books written in Greek between about 50 CE and the early second century: Paul's letters first, then the four Gospels (Mark, Matthew, Luke and John), the Acts of the Apostles, the other letters and Revelation. It is not written in the classical Attic of the schools but in Koine (κοινή, koinē, "common"), the everyday Greek of the eastern Roman empire, coloured by the Greek of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. Its style ranges widely. Mark tells his story in the present tense and moves it along with εὐθύς (euthys, "immediately"), some forty times. Luke opens with a single polished period (1:1–4) worthy of a Greek historian, as does the Letter to the Hebrews. Revelation bends grammar freely, as in ἀπὸ ὁ ὤν (apo ho ōn, "from the one who is", 1:4), where classical Greek requires a genitive after ἀπό.

For students of Greek it is a window onto the language people actually used in the first century, and it survives in more manuscripts than any other ancient text. The collection took shape gradually; the first list that matches our 27 books exactly is in a letter of Athanasius of Alexandria from 367 CE.

core.manuscripts: Nearly 6,000 Greek manuscripts are catalogued. They include some 140 papyri (P52, P46, P66 and P75 among the oldest), around 320 majuscules written in capitals on parchment (among them Codex Sinaiticus, ℵ; Vaticanus, B; Alexandrinus, A; Ephraemi Rescriptus, C; and Bezae, D), about 2,900 minuscules, and some 2,400 lectionaries, which arrange the text for reading in church. Early translations into Latin, Syriac and Coptic, and thousands of quotations in the Church Fathers, are witnesses too; this collection includes a Coptic version of Mark. Textual critics have traditionally grouped the manuscripts into text types: the Alexandrian (ℵ, B, P75), the 'Western' (D and the Old Latin) and the Byzantine, which accounts for most medieval copies. The Editio Critica Maior, begun in 1997, is now rebuilding the text with a computer-assisted method (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) that traces relationships between individual manuscripts rather than text types.
core.variants: Estimates run to several hundred thousand variant readings, almost all of them trivial: spelling, word order, small slips. The best-known exceptions are the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20), the story of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) and the 'Johannine Comma' (1 John 5:7–8), none of which is in the earliest witnesses, and the ending of Romans, whose closing doxology stands in different places in different manuscripts. The 'Western' text of Acts, represented by Codex Bezae, is almost a tenth longer than the Alexandrian. Modern critical editions (Nestle–Aland and the UBS Greek New Testament) reconstruct the text eclectically, relying mainly on the Alexandrian witnesses. The Textus Receptus behind the King James Version largely follows the Byzantine text.

core.summary:
Nonnus of Panopolis (Νόννος, Nonnos, fl. c. 450–470 CE) came from Panopolis in Upper Egypt, a centre of late Greek poetry. His Dionysiaca (Διονυσιακά), in forty-eight books and some 21,000 lines, is the longest poem to survive from antiquity. It tells the life of the god Dionysus, from the ancestry of Cadmus to his birth, his conquest of India, his travels and his reception among the gods, in a flood of mythological digressions, love stories and battles. Its forty-eight books match the combined total of the Iliad and the Odyssey, and the poem openly competes with Homer.

A hexameter Paraphrase of the Gospel of John is also transmitted under the name of Nonnus. Whether the same poet wrote both, and in what order, has long been debated; the older idea that he converted from paganism to Christianity is now doubted, since the two poems may have been written close together by a Christian poet at ease with pagan myth.

Nonnus' style is flamboyant, dense with compound adjectives and repeated images, and his hexameter follows strict rules of his own. He avoids many rhythms that Homer allowed and shapes the ends of lines to suit the stress accent of his day. He founded a school of late Greek epic, and his influence can be traced in poets such as Colluthus and Musaeus.

core.manuscripts: The Dionysiaca survives in a single medieval manuscript, Laurentianus 32.16 in Florence, written and annotated around 1280 by Maximus Planudes or his circle. All later copies derive from it. The Paraphrase of John has a separate tradition with many manuscripts.
core.variants: With a single manuscript, the text of the Dionysiaca depends heavily on conjecture, and Nonnus' strict metrical rules have been used to correct it. The authorship and relative date of the Paraphrase, and the date of Nonnus himself, are debated.

core.summary:
The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. Its name comes from the Latin for "seventy" (Greek Οἱ Ἑβδομήκοντα, hoi Hebdomēkonta, "the Seventy"; abbreviated LXX). It recalls the legend, told in the Letter of Aristeas, that seventy-two Jewish elders translated the Law at Alexandria for King Ptolemy II. The story is legendary, but the Pentateuch was in fact translated in Alexandria in the third century BCE, and the other books followed over the next two centuries. The grandson of Ben Sira, translating his grandfather's book around 132 BCE, already speaks of the Law, the Prophets and the other books as available in Greek.

The Septuagint was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and then of the early Church. The New Testament writers usually quote it, and it remains the Old Testament of the Greek Orthodox Church. It contains books and additions not in the Hebrew Bible, among them Wisdom, Ben Sira (Ecclesiasticus), Judith, Tobit, the books of Maccabees and additions to Esther and Daniel. Because it was translated from Hebrew texts older than the medieval Masoretic text, it is also an important witness to the Hebrew Bible itself.

Its Greek is Koine, but it varies greatly from book to book, from very literal renderings that follow Hebrew word order to free and idiomatic ones. Hebrew idiom shows through everywhere, as in the frequent καὶ ἐγένετο (kai egeneto, "and it came to pass"), and the Septuagint in turn shaped the language of the New Testament. Readers should note that the English translation offered here (the World English Bible) is made from the Hebrew, not from the Greek. It therefore often differs from the text beside it: the Greek Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew, and the Psalms are numbered differently.

core.manuscripts: The great fourth- and fifth-century Christian codices, Vaticanus (B), Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), are the most complete early witnesses. Hundreds of later manuscripts follow, many of them reflecting ancient revisions: the Hexaplaric text derived from Origen's work and the 'Lucianic' or Antiochian text. Papyri and fragments from Qumran and the Judaean desert take the evidence back to the second and first centuries BCE. Daughter translations into Latin, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and other languages are also important.
core.variants: There is no single Septuagint text: each book has its own translator, history and revisions. For Daniel, for example, the churches replaced the original Greek with the version attributed to Theodotion. Editions differ in their base: Swete's edition, used here, largely prints Codex Vaticanus with variants from other major manuscripts, while the Göttingen edition reconstructs the oldest recoverable text book by book. The order and number of books also differ between manuscripts and editions.

core.summary:
Origen (Ὠριγένης, Ōrigenēs, c. 185–c. 253 CE) was born in Alexandria to a Christian family. His father Leonides was executed in the persecution of 202. According to Eusebius, the young Origen soon headed the city's school of Christian instruction, lived a life of extreme asceticism, and even castrated himself, a report many historians doubt. After a conflict with his bishop, Demetrius, he moved to Caesarea in Palestine in the early 230s, where he was ordained a presbyter and taught for the rest of his life. He was imprisoned and tortured in the persecution of Decius (250) and died a few years later, probably at Tyre.

Origen was the first great Christian scholar and one of the most productive writers of antiquity. Ancient sources speak of thousands of works. He compiled the Hexapla, which set the Hebrew Old Testament and several Greek versions side by side in six columns, and wrote commentaries and homilies on almost every book of the Bible, a systematic theology (On First Principles), and a reply in eight books to the pagan critic Celsus (Against Celsus, c. 248). He read scripture on several levels, literal, moral and spiritual, which he compared to body, soul and spirit, and his allegorical method shaped Christian exegesis for centuries.

Some of his speculative ideas, such as the pre-existence of souls, were condemned in the sixth century, and much of his Greek work was lost as a result. Many writings survive only in the Latin translations of Rufinus and Jerome. His Greek is plain and workmanlike, the efficient Koine of a teacher and scholar rather than a stylist.

core.manuscripts: Each of Origen's works has its own history, and most of his output is lost. Against Celsus survives complete in one thirteenth-century manuscript, Vaticanus gr. 386, from which all other copies descend, supplemented by excerpts in the Philocalia. Much of his biblical commentary survives only as fragments in the Byzantine catenae, chains of extracts from different commentators. Discoveries still add to the corpus. Papyri from Tura (1941) preserved two lost works, and in 2012 Marina Molin Pradel identified twenty-nine Homilies on the Psalms in a twelfth-century Munich manuscript (Monacensis gr. 314).
core.variants: The main problem is authenticity and fidelity. Rufinus admitted that he softened passages in On First Principles that later readers found unorthodox, so the Latin cannot simply be taken as Origen's words. Catena fragments are often abbreviated or wrongly attributed. How far the sixth-century condemnations fairly represent his views is still debated.

core.summary:
Pausanias (Παυσανίας, Pausanias, fl. c. 150–180 CE) was a Greek traveller from Asia Minor, probably from Magnesia ad Sipylum in Lydia, and almost everything we know of him comes from his own book. His Description of Greece (Ἑλλάδος περιήγησις, Hellados periēgēsis) guides the reader, region by region, through mainland Greece: Attica, the Corinthia and Argolid, Laconia, Messenia, Elis and Olympia (two books), Achaea, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis with Delphi. Datable references show that he was writing between about 155 and 180 CE.

Pausanias chose what to describe. He passes over most Roman buildings and concentrates on the sanctuaries, temples, statues, paintings and tombs of the Greek past, with the myths, local histories and religious rites attached to them. He was little read in antiquity, but modern archaeology has made him indispensable. Excavators at Olympia, Delphi and Mycenae have used him as a guidebook, and his descriptions preserve works of art that are otherwise lost.

His Greek is his own. He imitates Herodotus in his digressions, his local stories and some Ionic turns of phrase, but his prose is deliberately varied and often awkward, with an unusual word order that makes him harder than he first appears. He is careful to say which things he has seen himself and which he has only been told, and those distinctions are a good guide to his method.

Begins his Description of Greece with Attica (c. 155)

Completes the work (c. 180)

core.manuscripts: All the surviving manuscripts, some twenty, were copied in Italy in the fifteenth century. They descend from a single archetype that the humanist Niccolò Niccoli had in Florence in 1418, which passed to the library of San Marco at his death in 1437 and was lost after 1500. The text therefore rests on one lost medieval witness, and its errors must be corrected by conjecture.
core.variants: The single archetype had many corruptions and gaps. Place names, inscriptions he quotes and numbers are frequently damaged. Pausanias' own reliability has been debated since the nineteenth century: some scholars accused him of copying earlier guidebooks rather than seeing things for himself, but excavations have repeatedly confirmed his descriptions.

core.summary:
Philo of Alexandria (Φίλων, Philōn, c. 20 BCE–c. 50 CE) belonged to a wealthy and prominent family in the largest Jewish community of the Greek-speaking world: his brother Alexander was a leading official, and his nephew Tiberius Julius Alexander abandoned Judaism and became prefect of Egypt. Philo was steeped both in the Jewish scriptures, which he read in the Greek of the Septuagint (how much Hebrew he knew is debated), and in Greek philosophy, especially Plato and the Stoics, and he spent his life explaining the one through the other.

Most of his roughly forty surviving Greek treatises interpret the five books of Moses, in three great series: an allegorical commentary on Genesis, an exposition of the Law, and a set of Questions and Answers that survives mainly in Armenian. Read allegorically, the stories of Genesis become lessons about the soul and its journey towards God. He also wrote an eyewitness account of the embassy he led to the emperor Gaius (Caligula) in 39–40 CE, after anti-Jewish riots in Alexandria; Josephus, the only near-contemporary to mention him, describes him leading it. His way of reading scripture through philosophy deeply influenced early Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria and Origen.

His Greek is rich, literary and close to classical models, with long, carefully built periods. Central to his thought is the divine λόγος (logos, "word, reason"), through which God creates and governs the world, a term whose relation to the opening of John's Gospel has been much discussed.
timeline: Born in Alexandria to a wealthy Jewish family

core.manuscripts: Philo survived because Christians, not Jews, copied him. The medieval Greek manuscripts, about sixty and none older than the tenth century (for example Vaticanus gr. 381 and Laurentianus 85.10), go back to the Christian library at Caesarea founded on Origen's books. A note in several of them records that Bishop Euzoius, in the later fourth century, had the library's worn papyrus rolls copied onto parchment codices. Two papyrus books, one from Coptos (third century) and one from Oxyrhynchus, give earlier evidence, and a sixth-century Armenian translation preserves works lost in Greek, including the Questions and Answers on Genesis and on Exodus.
core.variants: The titles and divisions of the treatises differ between manuscripts and from the list Eusebius gives. Some works transmitted under Philo's name are not his: On the World and the Latin Biblical Antiquities are spurious. On the Contemplative Life, which describes a community of Jewish ascetics near Alexandria, was once dismissed as a Christian forgery but is now generally accepted.

core.summary:
Flavius Philostratus (Φιλόστρατος, Philostratos, c. 170–c. 250 CE) came from a family of sophists on the island of Lemnos, studied at Athens, and became a member of the literary circle of the empress Julia Domna, wife of Septimius Severus. At her request he wrote the Life of Apollonius of Tyana, in eight books, about a first-century Pythagorean holy man and wonder-worker; it was completed after her death in 217. Pagan writers later set Apollonius up as a rival to Christ, and Eusebius wrote a reply. His Lives of the Sophists, written in the 230s, introduced the term 'Second Sophistic' (δευτέρα σοφιστική, deutera sophistikē) for the great age of Greek oratory from the first to the early third century CE, and it is our main source for that movement.

The other works under his name include the Heroicus, a dialogue in which a vine-grower near Troy reports the ghost of the hero Protesilaus correcting Homer; the Gymnasticus, on athletic training; and a collection of love letters. The Imagines, descriptions of sixty-five paintings in a villa near Naples, are ascribed to a Philostratus of Lemnos, often called the Elder, and a second, shorter Imagines to his grandson, the Younger. The ancient sources list several men of this name in one family. How they are related, and which works belong to which, is a notorious puzzle, and some scholars think the elder Imagines are by our Philostratus himself.

Philostratus writes in a lively, showy Atticising style, full of rare words, anecdote and description (ἔκφρασις, ekphrasis). The Imagines were a model for later writers on art.

A member of the circle of the empress Julia Domna (c. 205–217)

core.manuscripts: Each of the works has its own manuscript tradition. The Life of Apollonius and the Lives of the Sophists survive in many medieval copies, and the Imagines were popular in Byzantium and the Renaissance. Because the family's works were often copied together, attribution in the manuscripts is not always reliable.
core.variants: The main problem is authorship: the ancient Suda lists at least three Philostrati, and scholars disagree about which of them wrote the Imagines, the Heroicus, the Gymnasticus and the letters. The historical reliability of the Life of Apollonius, which claims to use the notes of Apollonius' companion Damis, is much debated; many scholars think Damis a literary invention.

core.summary:
Pindar of Thebes (Πίνδαρος, Pindaros, c. 518–c. 438 BCE) was, in Quintilian's judgement, "by far the first" of the nine canonical Greek lyric poets. He composed songs in many genres for choruses to sing and dance, but what survives nearly complete are his victory odes (ἐπινίκια, epinikia): four books celebrating winners at the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian games, commissioned by tyrants, kings and aristocratic families across the Greek world. The odes were probably sung and danced by a chorus, though some scholars have argued that at least some were performed solo.

A victory ode is not a sports report. Pindar sets the win beside myth, the victor's family and city and the gods, and draws from it reflections on human success and its limits: "Creatures of a day! What is anyone? What is no one? Man is a dream of a shadow" (ἐπάμεροι· τί δέ τις; τί δ᾽ οὔ τις; σκιᾶς ὄναρ ἄνθρωπος, Pythian 8.95–96). The other thirteen books of his poetry (hymns, paeans, dithyrambs, maiden-songs and more) are known only from papyri and quotations.

His Greek is famously difficult: bold metaphors, sudden transitions and complex metres, in a literary language with a Doric colouring (ᾱ for η, and Μοῖσα, Moisa, for Attic Μοῦσα, "Muse") and some Aeolic forms. The ancient commentaries (scholia), which preserve the work of Alexandrian scholars, are still a great help.

core.manuscripts: The four books of victory odes survive in about 180 medieval manuscripts, most descended from Byzantine editions; the end of the Isthmian book has been lost. The oldest, Ambrosianus C 222 inf. in Milan (A, twelfth century), contains only the Olympian odes; Vaticanus gr. 1312 (B, twelfth or thirteenth century) is the other key witness. In the twentieth century papyri from Oxyrhynchus, especially P.Oxy. 841 with the Paeans, recovered much of the rest of his poetry.
core.variants: Medieval copies set Pindar out in short metrical units (cola) that do not show how his stanzas are really built, so the metrical structure has had to be reconstructed; August Boeckh's edition of 1811 was the first to do this convincingly. Because each strophe and its antistrophe share exactly the same metre, that strict correspondence is still editors' main tool for detecting corruption.

core.summary:
Plato (Πλάτων, Platōn, c. 428–348 BCE) came from a leading Athenian family (his mother's cousin Critias and her brother Charmides were leaders of the oligarchy of the Thirty in 404), became a follower of Socrates, and after Socrates' execution in 399 BCE spent the rest of his life writing and teaching. Around 387 he founded the Academy, where Aristotle studied for twenty years. He almost never speaks in his own voice: his works are dialogues, most of them led by Socrates, and they are as much drama as philosophy.

The dialogues range from short, sharp conversations about courage or piety that end in ἀπορία (aporia, "perplexity", literally "no way through"), through great works such as the Symposium, Phaedo and Republic, with their theory of Forms (εἶδος or ἰδέα, eidos or idea), the immortal soul and the ideal city, to demanding late works such as the Sophist and the Laws. The usual grouping into early, middle and late dialogues is a modern reconstruction, based partly on counting features of style, and is not beyond dispute. Unusually for an ancient author, everything Plato is known to have published seems to survive, along with some works wrongly attributed to him.

His Attic prose is among the most beautiful in Greek, and it catches the rhythms of real conversation. Particles do much of the work, and Socrates' partners keep agreeing with formulas like πάνυ γε (panu ge, "very much so") and πάνυ μὲν οὖν (panu men oun, "certainly"). The early dialogues (Apology, Crito, Euthyphro) are a classic first step for students.

core.manuscripts: The medieval tradition rests on a few primary manuscripts. The oldest dated one is the Bodleian Library's Clarke 39 in Oxford (B), copied in 895 for Arethas of Caesarea and covering the first six tetralogies. Beside it stand a Venice manuscript (Marcianus App. Class. IV.1, T, mid-tenth century), a Vienna manuscript (Suppl. gr. 7, W, eleventh century) and, for the last two tetralogies including the Republic, Parisinus gr. 1807 (A, ninth century) and a later but independent Vienna manuscript (Suppl. gr. 39, F). The arrangement of the dialogues in nine groups of four (tetralogies) goes back to Thrasyllus in the first century CE. Papyri from the third century BCE onward preserve parts of many dialogues, sometimes with readings that differ from the medieval manuscripts.
core.variants:
Scholars debate whether several works in the collection are genuine. The First Alcibiades, the Greater Hippias, the Clitophon, the Epinomis and most of the Letters are doubted by many; the Seventh Letter, the most important of them, is itself much debated. The Second Alcibiades, the Minos and others are generally considered spurious, and a few short pieces were already classed as spurious in antiquity. Diogenes Laertius reports that the Laws was left on wax tablets and copied out by Plato's pupil Philip of Opus, who may also have written the Epinomis. The text of the Apology and Crito is comparatively secure. Some have argued that Book 1 of the Republic began life as a separate, earlier dialogue.

Passages are cited by Stephanus' page and section letter: Republic 514a, for example, is the opening of the Allegory of the Cave.

core.summary:
Plotinus (Πλωτῖνος, Plōtinos, 204/5–270 CE) is known to us almost entirely from the Life written by his pupil Porphyry. He was born in Egypt (a later writer, Eunapius, names Lycopolis). He turned to philosophy at twenty-eight and studied for eleven years at Alexandria with Ammonius Saccas. In 243 he joined the emperor Gordian III's campaign against Persia, hoping to learn the philosophy of the Persians and Indians. After the campaign failed he settled in Rome, where he taught for the rest of his life; he once asked the emperor Gallienus, in vain, to found a city of philosophers, 'Platonopolis'. He died in Campania in 270.

Plotinus saw himself as an interpreter of Plato, but modern scholars regard him as the founder of Neoplatonism. All reality, in his account, flows from a single source, the One (τὸ ἕν, to hen), through Intellect (νοῦς, nous) and Soul (ψυχή, psychē) down to the material world, and the soul's task is to turn back and rise to its origin. He began writing only at about fifty, in 253/4, and produced fifty-four treatises. After his death Porphyry arranged them by subject into six groups of nine, the Enneads (Ἐννεάδες, Enneades, from ἐννέα, "nine"), and published them around 301 with the Life. Through Porphyry, Augustine and Ficino his thought shaped late ancient, medieval and Renaissance philosophy, Christian, Jewish and Islamic alike.

His Greek is hard. Porphyry says that Plotinus wrote as he thought, never reread or corrected his work because of his weak eyes, and paid no attention to spelling (Life 8). The result is compressed, allusive prose that often reads like one side of a seminar discussion, with objections raised and answered in a few words. Most readers do best with a translation beside the Greek.

core.manuscripts: All the surviving manuscripts go back to a single archetype of Porphyry's edition. Paul Henry and Hans-Rudolf Schwyzer, whose edition was the first to rest on a full study of the tradition, sorted them into a few families. An ancient note (on Ennead IV.4.29) mentions an edition by another pupil, the physician Eustochius, and long passages quoted by Eusebius may derive from it. The Arabic 'Theology of Aristotle' is an independent, if very free, witness to parts of the text.
core.variants: Porphyry's arrangement is by subject, not by date, and it sometimes splits a single long work across several treatises. The so-called 'great treatise', for example, is divided among III.8, V.8, V.5 and II.9. The Life gives the order in which the treatises were written, and many readers now follow it. Plotinus' compressed style leaves many sentences open to more than one construction, so translations differ more than usual.

core.summary:
Plutarch (Πλούταρχος, Ploutarchos, c. 46–after 119 CE) spent most of his life in his small home town of Chaeronea in Boeotia, though he studied in Athens, visited Rome and Alexandria, held Roman citizenship as Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus, and served for many years as one of the two priests of Apollo at Delphi. He was a Platonist philosopher and an enormously productive writer. An ancient list of his works, the Lamprias catalogue, names 227 titles; about fifty Lives and some seventy-eight other works survive.

His Parallel Lives pair a Greek statesman or general with a Roman one (Alexander with Caesar, Demosthenes with Cicero) to explore character and moral example. As he puts it at the start of the Alexander, "it is not histories I am writing, but lives" (οὔτε γὰρ ἱστορίας γράφομεν, ἀλλὰ βίους). The Moralia gathers everything else: essays, dialogues and lectures on ethics, religion, education, politics, natural science and literature. Translated into French by Jacques Amyot and from Amyot into English by Thomas North, whose version Shakespeare used for his Roman plays, Plutarch was one of the most widely read Greek authors in Renaissance and early modern Europe.

His Greek is learned, leisurely Koine with a large vocabulary and long, balanced sentences. He is no strict Atticist, but like the classical orators he takes care to avoid hiatus.

core.manuscripts: The Lives come down in two arrangements, one in two volumes and one in three. Leading witnesses include two Paris manuscripts, Parisinus gr. 1671 (A, 1296) and Parisinus gr. 1672 (E, fourteenth century), the fullest single manuscript of Plutarch, together with Laurentianus 69.6 in Florence (L) and Marcianus gr. 385 in Venice. For the Moralia, the collection made by the Byzantine scholar Maximus Planudes around 1296 gave the corpus its shape.
core.variants: Not all the Lives survive. The pair Epaminondas and Scipio, which probably opened the series, is lost, as are several single Lives named in the Lamprias catalogue. Several works in the Moralia are not his, including On the Education of Children and the Lives of the Ten Orators. The order in which the pairs of Lives are transmitted is not Plutarch's own.

core.summary:
Polybius of Megalopolis (Πολύβιος, Polybios, c. 200–c. 118 BCE) was the son of a leading statesman of the Achaean League and himself a politician and cavalry commander of the League. After Rome's victory at Pydna in 168 BCE he was taken to Rome as one of a thousand Achaean detainees, held in Italy without trial for some seventeen years. There he became the friend and mentor of the young Scipio Aemilianus, and he was later present at the destruction of Carthage in 146.

His Histories, in forty books, set out to explain how the Romans came to rule almost the whole known world "in not quite fifty-three years" (220–167 BCE). Polybius calls his method πραγματικὴ ἱστορία (pragmatikē historia, "political and practical history"). He insists that history must be useful to statesmen and built on eyewitnesses, documents and first-hand knowledge of places and warfare, and he criticizes earlier historians sharply. Only Books 1–5 survive complete; the rest come in excerpts. His analysis in Book 6 of the Roman constitution as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy influenced Montesquieu and the founders of the American republic.

He writes the educated Koine of the Hellenistic age, not classical Attic: a prose rich in abstract nouns and the language of government and war, careful to avoid hiatus but indifferent to ornament. One word to watch is τύχη (tychē, "fortune"), the force he sees at work behind Rome's rise.

core.manuscripts: Books 1–5 survive complete in Vaticanus gr. 124 (A, tenth or eleventh century) and the manuscripts copied from it. Books 6–18 are known partly from a Byzantine selection of excerpts (the 'Excerpta Antiqua') in Urbinas gr. 102 (F, eleventh century). The rest comes from the collections of excerpts made in the tenth century for the emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, arranged by theme (on embassies, on virtues and vices, on sayings, on plots), and from quotations in Athenaeus, Strabo and others.
core.variants: Because so much of the text survives only in excerpts, the order and placement of the fragments of Books 6–40 are editors' reconstructions, and book numbers for fragments differ between editions. The reconstruction of Book 6 is particularly contested.

core.summary:
Porphyry (Πορφύριος, Porphyrios, 234–c. 305 CE) was born at Tyre in Phoenicia. His original name, Malchus, means "king" in his native Semitic language, and his teacher Longinus turned it into the Greek Porphyrios, "the purple one", after the royal colour. After studying with Longinus in Athens he joined Plotinus in Rome in 263. When he fell into a deep depression, Plotinus sent him to Sicily to recover. Around 301 he published Plotinus' treatises as the Enneads, with a Life of his teacher.

Porphyry was a prolific scholar and philosopher: he wrote some sixty works on philosophy, religion, literature, grammar and science. His Isagoge (Εἰσαγωγή, "Introduction"), a short guide to the terms used in Aristotle's Categories, became the first book of the logic curriculum for more than a thousand years. Its opening question about the status of genera and species set off the medieval debate over universals. His fifteen books Against the Christians were condemned and burned by imperial order in 448 and survive only in fragments. Among the works in this collection are his Life of Pythagoras, On Abstinence from Animal Food, a Letter to his wife Marcella, a commentary on the Categories in question-and-answer form, and his Homeric Questions.

His Greek is clear, orderly and learned, the prose of a teacher who wanted to be understood. He is much easier to read than Plotinus, and his introductions and letters are a good way into the language of late Greek philosophy.
timeline: Born at Tyre (234)

core.manuscripts: The Isagoge was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages and survives in a vast number of Greek manuscripts, as well as in Latin (Boethius), Syriac, Arabic and Armenian translations. The other works have much thinner traditions. The Homeric Questions have to be reconstructed from Byzantine collections and from scholia in the margins of Homer manuscripts. Against the Christians is known only from quotations and rebuttals by Christian writers.
core.variants: Many of Porphyry's works survive only in fragments whose extent and wording are disputed, and the attribution of some quotations, especially of passages thought to come from Against the Christians, is uncertain. The reconstruction of the Homeric Questions from the scholia is particularly difficult, because Byzantine compilers reworded and combined what they excerpted.

core.summary:
Proclus (Πρόκλος, Proklos, 412–485 CE) was born in Constantinople to a family from Lycia. After studying rhetoric and philosophy at Alexandria he came to Athens around 430 and studied with Plutarch of Athens and Syrianus. He succeeded Syrianus as head of the Platonic school at Athens, with the title διάδοχος (diadochos, "successor"), and led it for almost fifty years. His pupil Marinus wrote his biography, which portrays him as a pagan saint: tireless in teaching, writing and prayer.

Proclus gave Neoplatonism its most systematic form. His Elements of Theology derives the whole structure of reality from the One in 211 propositions, set out like a geometry book, and his Platonic Theology is a vast summa of pagan theology. He wrote long commentaries on Plato's Timaeus, Republic, Parmenides, Alcibiades and Cratylus, and on the first book of Euclid, as well as hymns to the gods. His ideas reached the Middle Ages through the Christian writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius and through the Book of Causes, an Arabic adaptation of the Elements of Theology later translated into Latin. The commentary on the Republic in this collection is the only sustained ancient commentary on that dialogue.

The second work here, the Chrestomathy, is a summary of the lost poems of the Epic Cycle, preserved in manuscripts of Homer. It is transmitted under the name Proclus, but most scholars doubt that the philosopher wrote it and think it the work of an otherwise unknown grammarian, perhaps of the second century CE. Proclus' own Greek is technical and scholastic, with long sentences built around the triad of μονή, πρόοδος, ἐπιστροφή (monē, proodos, epistrophē: "remaining, procession, reversion"), the pattern by which everything flows from its cause and returns to it.
timeline: Born at Constantinople (412)
Comes to Athens to study with Plutarch and Syrianus (c. 430)
Succeeds Syrianus as head of the Platonic school
Dies at Athens

core.manuscripts: The Commentary on the Republic survives in essence in a single damaged early manuscript, Laurentianus 80.9 in Florence, and parts of the text are lost or can be read only with difficulty. The Chrestomathy's summaries of the Epic Cycle survive in the prefaces of Homer manuscripts, above all the tenth-century Venetus A; the Byzantine scholar Photius summarised the rest of the work in his Library.
core.variants: Because the Republic commentary depends so heavily on one damaged manuscript, editors have had to supply many readings, and later Byzantine copies help only a little. The authorship of the Chrestomathy is disputed, as is how faithfully its summaries reflect the lost epics, which may have been shortened or rearranged to fit around the Iliad and Odyssey.

core.summary:
Procopius of Caesarea (Προκόπιος, Prokopios, c. 500–after 554 CE) was born in Caesarea in Palestine and trained as a lawyer. From 527 he served as legal adviser and secretary to Belisarius, Justinian's great general, and went with him on campaign against the Persians, the Vandals in North Africa (533–534) and the Goths in Italy (535–540). He was an eyewitness of much of what he describes. The date of his death is unknown.

His Wars (Ὑπὲρ τῶν πολέμων, Hyper tōn polemōn), in eight books, recount Justinian's campaigns in the East, Africa and Italy; the first seven books were published around 551 and the eighth a few years later. His Buildings praises the emperor's building programme across the empire. The Secret History (Ἀνέκδοτα, Anekdota, "Unpublished things"), written around 550 and not meant for circulation in his lifetime, attacks Justinian, the empress Theodora and Belisarius with astonishing venom. The contrast between the public and private works has made Procopius one of the most discussed writers of late antiquity. The Secret History was first printed in 1623 from Vatican manuscripts, and its authenticity, once doubted, is now generally accepted.

Procopius wrote in classicising Greek modelled on Herodotus and Thucydides. He avoided the everyday Latin and Christian vocabulary of his time, often explaining such terms with a circumlocution as if they were foreign to his readers. His descriptions of the plague of 542 in Constantinople and of the Nika riots of 532 are among the most famous passages of Byzantine prose.

core.manuscripts: The Wars survive in a number of medieval manuscripts in two main families, and the Buildings has its own tradition. The Secret History was little copied. It was known in Byzantium (the tenth-century Suda cites it), but survives in only a few late manuscripts, from which Alemanni made the first edition in 1623.
core.variants: The dating of Procopius' works, especially the Buildings, is debated, and so is how his hostility in the Secret History should be reconciled with the praise of the Buildings. Some scholars once thought the Secret History a later forgery, but its language and knowledge are Procopius' own. The Buildings says almost nothing about Italy, which suggests it was left unfinished.

core.summary:
Quintus of Smyrna (Κόϊντος Σμυρναῖος, Koïntos Smyrnaios, probably 3rd century CE) is known only from his poem. In one passage (Book 12) he claims that the Muses inspired him while he tended sheep near Smyrna, echoing Hesiod's meeting with the Muses. That is all he tells us. Most scholars date him to the third century, though some prefer the fourth.

His Posthomerica (Τὰ μεθ᾽ Ὅμηρον, Ta meth' Homēron, "The Events after Homer"), in fourteen books, fills the gap between the end of the Iliad and the beginning of the Odyssey. It tells the story of the Amazon Penthesilea and the Ethiopian Memnon, the death of Achilles, the contest for his armour and the suicide of Ajax, the arrival of Neoptolemus and Philoctetes, the wooden horse, the sack of Troy and the departure of the Greeks. It is our only complete Greek epic account of these events, which were told in the lost poems of the Epic Cycle.

Quintus imitates Homer closely in language, formulas and similes, but his tone is more reflective and his gods more remote. He is sometimes called Quintus Calaber because the manuscript from which his poem became known was found by Cardinal Bessarion in a monastery near Otranto, in southern Italy, in the mid-fifteenth century.
timeline: The Posthomerica written (probably 3rd century CE)

core.manuscripts: All surviving manuscripts of the Posthomerica are of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and derive from the lost manuscript found by Bessarion at the monastery of San Nicola di Casole near Otranto.
core.variants: Because all the manuscripts go back to one lost exemplar, the text has many gaps and corruptions. The date of the poem is debated, and so is how far Quintus drew directly on the lost Cyclic epics, rather than on later handbooks, tragedy and Latin poetry such as Virgil's.

core.summary:
Sextus Empiricus (Σέξτος Ἐμπειρικός, Sextos Empeirikos, fl. c. 200 CE) was a doctor and a Pyrrhonist sceptic. His surname means that he belonged to the Empiric school of medicine, which relied on experience rather than theory. Almost nothing else is known about him: his date is inferred from the authors he mentions and from later references, and even where he lived and taught is unknown.

His surviving works are the Outlines of Pyrrhonism (Πυρρώνειοι ὑποτυπώσεις, Pyrrhōneioi hypotypōseis), in three books, and the larger treatise known as Against the Professors (Πρὸς μαθηματικούς, Pros mathēmatikous). The latter contains six books attacking the liberal arts (grammar, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astrology and music) and five against the dogmatic philosophers. Sextus sets out the sceptic's method: for every argument an equal and opposite argument can be found, so the sceptic suspends judgement (ἐποχή, epochē) and thereby reaches tranquillity (ἀταραξία, ataraxia). In doing so he records the arguments of many earlier philosophers whose works are lost, and he is our main source for ancient scepticism.

His Greek is plain and technical. When his Outlines were translated into Latin and printed in 1562, they had an extraordinary effect on modern philosophy, from Montaigne to Descartes and Hume.
timeline: Active as a sceptic philosopher and Empiric physician (c. 200)
A medieval Latin translation of the Outlines circulates (14th century)

core.manuscripts: The Greek manuscripts are all late, of the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, and go back to a single lost archetype. A medieval Latin translation of the Outlines, made from a Greek manuscript older than any that survive, is an important independent witness.
core.variants: With a narrow tradition the text contains many corruptions and has been repaired by conjecture. The numbering of Against the Professors is confusing: the five books against the dogmatists are often cited as books 7–11, continuing the six against the arts, though they may originally have been a separate work. Scholars debate how original Sextus was, and how far he simply compiled earlier sceptical handbooks.

core.summary:
Simplicius (Σιμπλίκιος, Simplikios, c. 480–c. 560 CE) came from Cilicia and studied with Ammonius at Alexandria and with Damascius, the last head of the Platonic school at Athens. When the emperor Justinian stopped pagans from teaching philosophy in 529, Simplicius, Damascius and five other philosophers went to the court of the Persian king Khosrow I. They returned in 532, when a peace treaty between Rome and Persia guaranteed their freedom to live by their beliefs. Where Simplicius then lived and wrote is unknown; one theory places him at Harran in Mesopotamia, but it is disputed.

His commentaries on Aristotle's Categories, Physics and On the Heavens, and on Epictetus' Handbook, are among the longest and most learned works of ancient philosophy. They are also a treasury of quotations. Simplicius copied out long passages of earlier philosophers because, he said, their books had become rare. Much of what we have of the Presocratics comes from him, including the longest surviving portions of Parmenides' poem and important fragments of Empedocles and Anaxagoras. The commentary on Aristotle's On the Soul transmitted under his name may be by his contemporary Priscian of Lydia.

Simplicius wrote clear, careful scholarly Greek, and his commentaries show the last generation of pagan philosophers defending the harmony of Plato and Aristotle against Christian critics such as John Philoponus.

Dies (c. 560)
core.manuscripts: Each commentary survives in several medieval manuscripts. Because the commentaries quote earlier philosophers at length, their manuscripts are also the main witnesses for many Presocratic fragments, and editors of Parmenides or Empedocles must rely on Simplicius' text.
core.variants: The authorship of the commentary on On the Soul is disputed; many scholars now assign it to Priscian of Lydia. The quotations of the Presocratics sometimes differ from other sources, and editors must decide whether Simplicius had a better text or has miscopied. His whereabouts after 532, and the idea of a surviving Platonic school at Harran, remain debated.

core.summary:
Sophocles (Σοφοκλῆς, Sophoklēs, c. 497–406 BCE) spent his long life in Athens, where he was a public figure as well as a dramatist: he served as a treasurer of the Athenian empire and as a general alongside Pericles, and after his death he was honoured with a hero cult. He wrote more than 120 plays and was the most successful of the three great tragedians in competition, winning first prize eighteen or twenty-four times (the ancient sources differ) and, it was said, never coming last.

Seven of his tragedies survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Oedipus the King, Women of Trachis, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus, which was staged after his death. Aristotle's Poetics treats Oedipus the King as the model of a tragic plot. Sophocles' heroes are proud, stubborn people who will not bend, and his plays show what that costs them. A large part of a satyr play, the Trackers, was recovered from a papyrus in the twentieth century.

His Greek is lucid on the surface and full of double meanings beneath, which suits a dramatist of irony. The famous ode in the Antigone begins πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει (polla ta deina kouden anthrōpou deinoteron pelei, 332–33), and δεινός (deinos) means both "wonderful" and "terrible": "Many things are wondrous and dreadful, and none more so than man." As in all tragedy, the choral songs have a Doric colouring.

core.manuscripts: The same Florentine manuscript that preserves Aeschylus, Laurentianus 32.9 (L, tenth century), is the principal witness, with a palimpsest in Leiden (BPG 60A, around 950). Three plays, Ajax, Electra and Oedipus the King, formed the Byzantine school 'triad' and survive in nearly 200 manuscripts; the other four in far fewer. Parisinus gr. 2712 (A, thirteenth century) is an important independent witness. The Trackers survives only on a second-century CE papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, published in 1912.
core.variants: Editors disagree about how independent L and A are, and about the value of Demetrius Triclinius' fourteenth-century edition. The date of the Antigone rests on a doubtful ancient story that its success won Sophocles his generalship. Some passages have long been suspected as interpolations, above all Antigone 904–920, where Antigone argues that she would not have done for a husband or a child what she did for her brother. Goethe hoped that passage would be proved spurious, but Aristotle already quotes it in the Rhetoric, and most modern editors keep it.

core.summary:
Strabo (Στράβων, Strabōn, 64/63 BCE–c. 24 CE) came from Amaseia in Pontus, in northern Asia Minor, from a family that had served the kings of Pontus. He studied with the grammarian Tyrannion and the Aristotelian Xenarchus, leaned towards Stoic philosophy, and spent long periods in Rome. In 25–24 BCE he travelled up the Nile to the border of Ethiopia with his friend Aelius Gallus, the prefect of Egypt. His Historical Sketches, a continuation of Polybius in forty-seven books, are lost.

His Geography (Γεωγραφικά, Geōgraphika), in seventeen books, is the only large work of ancient geography to survive nearly complete. Books 1–2 set out his principles and criticise earlier geographers, especially Eratosthenes. Books 3–10 describe Europe from Iberia to Greece, Books 11–16 Asia, and Book 17 Egypt and Libya. Strabo wrote for statesmen, not specialists. He mixes physical description with history, myth, local customs and the famous men of each city, and he treats Homer as the founder of geography, defending the accuracy of his descriptions. The work was barely read in antiquity and was first widely used by Byzantine scholars. It was completed late in his life, after 18 CE.

His Greek is the plain, educated prose of the Augustan age, easy to follow but not elegant. The long quotations from earlier writers make the Geography a treasure-house of lost works.

core.manuscripts: The oldest evidence is a fifth-century palimpsest in the Vatican (Vat. gr. 2306 with 2061A), fragmentary but independent of the medieval tradition. For the first nine books the chief witness is a tenth-century Paris manuscript (Parisinus gr. 1397, A). For the last eight we depend on later manuscripts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. A Byzantine epitome and the excerpts known as the Chrestomathy, included in this collection, sometimes preserve readings lost elsewhere.
core.variants: The text has gaps, especially at the end of Book 7, which survives only in fragments preserved in the epitome and the Chrestomathy. The Aldine edition was printed from a poor manuscript, and its errors persisted in later editions until the manuscripts were collated afresh. Place names and numbers are often corrupt. Scholars also debate when and where Strabo wrote the work, at Rome or at home in Amaseia, and how far he revised it.

core.summary:
Theocritus (Θεόκριτος, Theokritos, active in the early third century BCE) came from Syracuse in Sicily and worked on the island of Cos and at the court of Ptolemy II in Alexandria. He is the inventor of pastoral poetry. His Idylls (the name, from εἰδύλλιον, eidyllion, "short piece", was given later) are hexameter poems in which herdsmen compete in song, lovers pine, and the countryside of Sicily and Cos is lovingly evoked.

The collection is wider than pastoral. It includes mimes of city life, such as the Syracusan Women (Idyll 15), where two housewives push through the crowds of Alexandria to a festival of Adonis; short epics about heroes; and poems in praise of Hieron II of Syracuse and Ptolemy II. Virgil's Eclogues answer Theocritus directly, and through Virgil he became the founder of the whole European pastoral tradition.

Most of the Idylls are written in a literary Doric, though a few use Aeolic or epic Ionic. The first line of Idyll 1 shows the flavour: Ἁδύ τι τὸ ψιθύρισμα καὶ ἁ πίτυς, αἰπόλε, τήνα (Hady ti to psithyrisma kai ha pitys, aipole, tēna, "Sweet is the whispering of that pine, goatherd"), with ἁδύ and ἁ where Attic has ἡδύ and ἡ, and τήνα for ἐκείνη, "that".
timeline: Born at Syracuse (approximate)

His latest datable poems belong to the 270s; nothing is known of his death

Editio princeps of Idylls 1–18 (Milan, c. 1480); Aldine 1495
core.manuscripts: The Idylls survive together with the other bucolic poets, Moschus and Bion, in three families of manuscripts: the Ambrosian (Ambrosianus C 222 inf., K, thirteenth century), the Vatican (Vaticanus gr. 915 and related manuscripts) and the Laurentian (Laurentianus 32.16 and 32.37). Papyri, notably the Antinoë papyrus (fifth century CE) with its ancient commentary, confirm the ancient text. Scribes often normalized Theocritus' Doric forms.
core.variants: Most editors regard Idylls 8, 9, 19, 20, 21, 23, 25 and 27 as not by Theocritus, while the poem for Ptolemy (Idyll 17) and the Syracusan Women (15) are securely his. The Syrinx, a pattern poem laid out in the shape of a panpipe, is also of doubtful authorship. Editions differ markedly in how much Doric colouring they restore.

core.summary:
Theophrastus of Eresus on Lesbos (Θεόφραστος, Theophrastos, c. 371–287 BCE) was Aristotle's closest colleague and his successor as head of the Lyceum, which he led for some thirty-five years, reportedly with about two thousand students. Diogenes Laertius says his real name was Tyrtamus, and that Aristotle renamed him Theophrastus, roughly "divine speaker", for the grace of his speech.

Like Aristotle he wrote on almost everything, but two achievements have lasted. His Enquiry into Plants and On the Causes of Plants describe and classify some five hundred plants, from Greece to India (drawing on reports from Alexander's campaigns), and founded botany as a science; Book 9 of the Enquiry, on medicinal plants and their uses, is an important early text of ancient pharmacology. His Characters, thirty sharp sketches of social types (the Flatterer, the Chatterbox, the Penny-pincher), were imitated from La Bruyère onward and have influenced European literature ever since. His short work On the Senses is also one of our main sources for what the Presocratic philosophers thought about perception.

Each of the Characters opens with a definition and then a portrait built on one formula: "the Flatterer is the sort of man who …", τοιοῦτός τις, οἷος … (toioutos tis, hoios …), followed by a run of infinitives describing what he does. The sketches are full of the everyday vocabulary of fourth-century Athens, the market, the assembly and the dinner party, and they are excellent reading practice.
timeline: Born at Eresus on Lesbos
With Aristotle at Assos and Lesbos
Succeeds Aristotle as head of the Lyceum
Characters (probable date)
Briefly leaves Athens when a law restricts the philosophical schools; returns the next year when it is repealed
Dies; bequeaths Aristotle's library to Neleus of Scepsis

core.manuscripts: The Enquiry into Plants rests chiefly on Urbinas gr. 61 in the Vatican (U, tenth or eleventh century) and a fifteenth-century Paris manuscript (Parisinus gr. 2069, P). Theodore Gaza's Latin translation, printed in 1483, was made from a manuscript now lost and sometimes preserves better readings. The Characters have a separate and complicated history: Byzantine excerptors split the sketches into two groups (1–15 and 16–30) that were copied separately.
core.variants: The order of the books of the Enquiry is disputed, and Book 9, on medicinal plants, may include later material. Many plant names are corrupt in the manuscripts, and some identifications remain uncertain. In Byzantine times the Characters were padded with moralizing introductions and conclusions, and given a spurious dedicatory preface, which editors now remove. The short weather-lore treatise On Weather Signs is probably by a later member of the school.

core.summary:
Thucydides (Θουκυδίδης, Thoukydidēs, c. 460–c. 400 BCE) was an Athenian who lived through the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BCE). He set out to record it from the very beginning, convinced it would be the greatest war yet. He caught the plague that struck Athens in 430 and survived it. In 424, as a general, he failed to save the city of Amphipolis and was exiled for twenty years, which gave him time, and access to both sides.

His history is analytical and austere. He looks for the real causes behind events, naming Sparta's fear of Athens' growing power as "the truest cause" (ἀληθεστάτη πρόφασις, alēthestatē prophasis, 1.23) of the war. He gives his speakers set-piece speeches that lay bare the arguments of each moment, among them Pericles' Funeral Oration and the Melian Dialogue, and he meant the whole to be "a possession for all time" (κτῆμα ἐς αἰεί, ktēma es aiei, 1.22). The narrative breaks off in 411 BCE; Xenophon's Hellenica and other historians picked up the story.

His Greek is famously compressed and difficult, full of abstract nouns, neuter participles used as nouns, and sentences that pack antithesis into antithesis. It is also an older Attic than Plato's: he writes ξύν (xyn) for σύν ("with") and -σσ- where later Attic has -ττ-, as in the first sentence of the work, Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον ("Thucydides the Athenian wrote up the war").
timeline: Born in Athens, of a family with Thracian connections
Outbreak of the Peloponnesian War; begins his record
Catches and survives the plague at Athens

End of the Peloponnesian War; Thucydides probably returns to Athens
Dies, the work unfinished
Lorenzo Valla completes his Latin translation for Pope Nicholas V
Aldine editio princeps
Thomas Hobbes publishes the first English translation made directly from the Greek
core.manuscripts: Seven primary manuscripts of the tenth to fourteenth centuries survive: Laurentianus 69.2 in Florence (C, tenth century), Vaticanus gr. 126 (B, eleventh century), Parisinus gr. 1734 (A), Palatinus gr. 252 in Heidelberg (E), two Munich manuscripts (Monacensis gr. 430, F, and gr. 228, G, the latter much later) and British Library Add. 11727 (M). They fall into two families, ABEFM and CG, though in the last books B follows an independent source of its own. Papyri, notably P.Oxy. 16 and 17, show a text very close to the medieval one.
core.variants: The division into eight books was made by later editors, not by Thucydides; ancient readers also knew divisions into nine and thirteen books. Book 8, and parts of Book 5, have no speeches in direct form and seem unrevised. The grim chapter on civil war at Corcyra, 3.84, is rejected by most editors, as it already was by ancient commentators. The speeches, with their strained syntax, still contain sentences whose exact wording is uncertain despite centuries of emendation.

core.summary:
Xenophon of Athens (Ξενοφῶν, Xenophōn, c. 430–after 355 BCE) was a soldier, landowner and writer, and a devoted follower of Socrates. In 401 BCE he joined the Greek mercenaries hired by the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger to seize his brother's throne. When Cyrus was killed at Cunaxa and the Greek generals were then murdered, Xenophon helped lead the Ten Thousand on an epic retreat through the mountains to the Black Sea, the story he tells in the Anabasis; its most famous moment is the soldiers' shout of θάλαττα θάλαττα (thalatta thalatta, "the sea! the sea!", 4.7.24) when they finally see it. Exiled from Athens, he lived for years on an estate near Olympia given to him by the Spartans.

He wrote in many forms: history (the Hellenica, which continues Thucydides, opening simply "After this …"), memoir (the Anabasis), Socratic works (the Memorabilia, Symposium, Oeconomicus and his own Apology), an idealized life of the Persian king Cyrus the Great (the Cyropaedia), and treatises on horsemanship, hunting, finance and running an estate.

Ancient critics admired the sweetness of his style; Diogenes Laertius says he was called "the Attic Muse". His Attic is clear and plain, though it admits poetic and non-Attic words that later purists frowned on, a hint of the Koine to come. That clarity made the Anabasis the first real Greek text for generations of students.

core.manuscripts: The manuscript tradition differs from work to work. For the Anabasis the chief witnesses are Parisinus gr. 1640 (C, 1320) and an older family represented by Vaticanus gr. 1335 (A) and Vaticanus gr. 987 (B). For the Hellenica they are Parisinus gr. 1738 (B) and Marcianus gr. 368 (M). Numerous papyri survive, a sign of Xenophon's popularity in schools.
core.variants: The Constitution of the Athenians, transmitted among Xenophon's works, is by an unknown earlier writer nicknamed 'the Old Oligarch', and Xenophon's authorship of On Hunting (Cynegeticus) is doubted. The short summaries at the start of several books of the Anabasis are later additions. In the Hellenica (3.1.2) Xenophon refers readers to an account of the expedition by 'Themistogenes of Syracuse', probably a pen-name for himself. The uneven quality of the Hellenica has led to theories that it was written in stages.

core.summary:
Xenophon of Ephesus (Ξενοφῶν Ἐφέσιος, Xenophōn Ephesios, probably 2nd century CE) is known only from his novel and a short notice in the Byzantine Suda. His name, like the novel's style, may be a tribute to the classical Xenophon. A reference to a police official in Cilicia, apparently the eirenarch, an office first attested under Trajan, suggests a date in the second century CE.

The Ephesian Tale (Ἐφεσιακά, Ephesiaka), in five books, tells how two beautiful young Ephesians, Habrocomes and Anthia, fall in love at a festival of Artemis, marry, and are separated on a voyage. Through pirates, shipwreck, slavery, brothels, attempted murders and unwanted suitors in Asia Minor, Egypt, Italy and Sicily, each stays faithful to the other until they are reunited at Rhodes. The plot is crowded with incident, and the pace rarely slows.

Xenophon's Greek is the simplest of all the novels: short sentences strung together with καί (kai, "and"), few subordinate clauses, repeated formulas and little description. Some scholars have taken this bareness, and the Suda's statement that the novel had ten books rather than five, as signs that our text is an abridgement. Others think the Suda's number is a simple error and that Xenophon wrote in a deliberately plain, popular style.
timeline: The office of eirenarch, apparently mentioned in the novel, is first attested under Trajan (98–117)
The Ephesian Tale written (probably 2nd century CE)

core.manuscripts: The Ephesian Tale survives only in the thirteenth-century Laurentianus Conventi Soppressi 627 in Florence (F), the same manuscript that preserves Chariton. All other copies derive from it, and no papyrus of the novel has yet been identified.
core.variants: With a single manuscript, the text contains many corruptions and some gaps that can only be repaired by conjecture. The chief debate is whether the novel is an epitome of a longer original, as some nineteenth-century scholars argued. Many now doubt it, explaining the Suda's 'ten books' as a copying error for 'five'.

core.summary:
Zosimus (Ζώσιμος, Zōsimos, fl. c. 500 CE) is described in the title of his work as a count and a former advocate of the treasury. He wrote after 498, since he mentions the abolition of a tax in that year, and he was a pagan in an empire that had long been Christian. Nothing else is known of him.

His New History (Ἱστορία νέα, Historia nea), in six books, runs from a brief sketch of Augustus and the early empire to a detailed account of the fourth century and the years up to 410, breaking off just before Alaric's sack of Rome. As the Greek historian Polybius had explained Rome's rise, Zosimus set out to explain its decline, which he blamed on the abandonment of the old gods and above all on Constantine. He relied closely on two lost historians, Eunapius for the period up to 404 and Olympiodorus after that; the Byzantine scholar Photius remarked that he had copied rather than written his history.

His value lies in what he preserves of his lost sources and in his rare pagan view of the Christian empire. His Greek is plain and straightforward, with little of the classicising display of his contemporaries.
timeline: Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge, which Zosimus treats as the start of Rome's decline

core.manuscripts: The New History survives in a single medieval manuscript, Vaticanus gr. 156, probably copied at the Studios monastery in Constantinople in the tenth or eleventh century. All other copies derive from it. The work is incomplete: the end of Book 6 is lost, and the text breaks off in the year 410.
core.variants: With a single manuscript, errors can only be corrected by conjecture, and lost leaves have left gaps, the largest between Books 1 and 2, where the years 282–305, including the reign of Diocletian, are missing. Scholars debate whether Zosimus left the work unfinished or whether its end was lost, and how closely each section reproduces Eunapius or Olympiodorus.
